parts.ask: Case 'Increasing public sector debt is a good policy' (UK, June 2020: borrowing five times June 2019; public sector debt 99.6% of GDP, highest for 60 years; Fig. 1 UK public sector net borrowing May 2019-Mar 2020, a line rising from about GBP 10bn to a peak of about GBP 56bn in Jan 2020, dipping to about GBP 48bn and ending near GBP 55bn; approximate reading of a 150 dpi page render; Japan's debt ratio over 200%). State what is meant by 'a recession'.
parts.final_form: definition with three elements: GDP/output, negative growth (a fall), time period (two successive quarters)
parts.ms: 1 linked to GDP; 1 negative growth of GDP/output; 1 over 2 quarters (MS p.8)
parts.er: Many missed one of the three elements and described things associated with a recession (high unemployment, low investment) instead; 'This is not what the question required' (PER 2023-03 p.8).

parts.ask: Analyse why governments borrow and why a government is said to need to increase spending in a recession.
parts.final_form: two linked explanations: borrowing finances spending not covered by tax (a deficit); extra G raises income, output, employment via the multiplier
parts.ms: 2 borrowing finances expenditure not covered by receipts/taxation; 1 finances a deficit; then 1 each: borrowing used to raise government spending/AMD, which raises income, output, employment, through the multiplier, encouraging growth (max 5) (MS p.8)
parts.er: Answered well; many gained at least 4/5. Expected: borrowing covers spending not met by tax revenue, and extra spending raises income, output and employment, which with the multiplier stimulates growth and offsets the recession (PER 2023-03 pp.8-9).

parts.ask: Consider what is meant by the claim that government borrowing could 'crowd out' the private sector (the article says this is a risk near full capacity, not in a recession).
parts.final_form: definition plus the process chain: bond sales -> higher interest rates -> dearer private borrowing -> less private investment and consumption
parts.ms: 2 definition: growth of government spending transfers scarce resources or finance from the private to the public sector; 1 government sells bonds to the private sector; 1 this may need higher interest rates (or stops private funds going to other projects); 1 private borrowing becomes dearer; 1 private investment and consumption crowded out (MS p.8)
parts.er: Either the resource-transfer or the funds-transfer explanation was accepted; candidates then had to explain the process: sale of government securities, rise in interest rates, dearer borrowing, crowding out of private investment (PER 2023-03 p.9).

parts.ask: Assess whether the article's evidence makes a conclusive case that the high level of government borrowing is an effective policy.
parts.final_form: two-sided assessment using only article evidence (including Fig. 1); 1 mark reserved for the conclusion that the evidence is inconclusive
parts.ms: 1 each: sound because the economy is in recession so no crowding out; cutting spending would worsen the position and government revenue; high debt acceptable if the debt/GDP ratio is stable, but Fig. 1 shows it was not stable and it is the highest for 60 years; Japan has no problem, but it is a different economy; borrowing may raise interest rates and deter investment; conclusion 'Evidence is inconclusive' (1, reserved) (MS p.8)
parts.er: Comments not based on the article gained no marks. Credit went to the interest-rate risk, the stability of the debt/GDP ratio and the point that the safe ratio differs by type of economy. Very few used Fig. 1 to show the ratio was not stable. Good answers split the evidence into for and against; one mark reserved for an acceptable conclusion (PER 2023-03 p.9).

parts.ask: Section B essay: air travel causes market failure through negative externalities. With the help of a diagram, assess how far a government can intervene to correct this market failure.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far intervention can correct the failure
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: market failure as allocative inefficiency (allocative efficiency where AR = MC); negative externality = cost to society greater than the private cost ('spill-over'); labelled diagram comparing the market and the allocatively efficient number of flights, with the welfare loss; interventions: taxation (raises the cost of air travel, fewer flights), negative advertising, direct regulation. AO3: the right tax is hard to measure; a tax may take time to work; advertising is costly and may not persuade enough; net effect of intervention not always positive; some interventions suit some goods better (MS pp.9-10). No diagram cap is printed for this question.
parts.er: Very popular. Air travel is a negative externality of consumption, not production; many drew a production-externality diagram, so diagrams and the analysis built on them were inaccurate, which blocked Level 3 (accurate analytical tools needed). Candidates had to judge how effective each intervention would be; at least 4/6 AO3 was possible for a fully developed conclusion (PER 2023-03 p.9).

parts.ask: Section B essay: some oligopolists collude rather than compete on price, which will lead to higher prices and a less efficient allocation of resources. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether collusion, on balance, raises prices and reduces efficiency
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: characteristics of oligopoly; collusion compared with price competition; meaning of an efficient allocation; analysis linking collusion, higher prices and allocative efficiency; price and non-price competition; X-inefficiency in large dominant firms. AO3: larger colluding firms may offer more choice; collusion may raise dynamic efficiency, investment and long-run lower prices (diagram possible); economies of scale; regulation can deal with harmful effects afterwards; judgement on the net effect on prices and efficiency (MS pp.11-12)
parts.er: Not dealt with effectively. Most described oligopoly and collusion (lower Level 2) but did not analyse collusion moving the market towards monopoly-type outcomes for price and efficiency, so most stayed at or below 8/14. Very few questioned the statement, so few gained AO3 marks; 'evaluate' requires testing the validity of the statement (PER 2023-03 pp.9-10).

parts.ask: Section C essay: expenditure-reducing policies will reduce a balance of payments deficit but will also cause significant unemployment. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on both halves of the statement, especially whether unemployment is 'significant'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: expenditure-reducing policies defined through the link between AD and import demand; examples (higher interest rates, deflationary fiscal policy); which type of unemployment may follow; how each instrument cuts the deficit (e.g. higher rates -> lower investment -> lower spending including imports); effect on unemployment. AO3: depends on the state of the economy (with high inflation and a positive output gap the effect on unemployment is limited); depends on the cause of existing unemployment; supply-side measures alongside may cut structural unemployment; spending may switch from imports to domestic goods (MS p.13)
parts.er: About half chose it. Better answers linked lower aggregate monetary demand to fewer imports and to (mainly cyclical) unemployment; two chains of reasoning on unemployment were needed for Level 3. Many did not question 'significant unemployment'; analysing the policies is not evaluation. Expected: impact depends on the state of the economy, the type of unemployment, substitution towards domestic goods (PER 2023-03 p.10).

parts.ask: Section C essay: assess the impact of globalisation on the standard of living in low-income countries.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the overall impact, using a living-standards measure that is not only material
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: globalisation = free trade, free movement of capital and labour, technology transfer, cultural/political ties; characteristics of low-income countries (low productivity, high dependency ratios, low GDP per head, primary exports); signs of low living standards (poverty, inequality, poor housing, education, health, fast population growth); living standards linked to GDP per head and productivity; trade and technology create real wealth; more tax revenue for health, housing, education. AO3: link to living standards unclear, labour exploitation; dependency and trade imbalances; skilled work done by imported labour so no local training; local firms outcompeted -> unemployment; conclusion depends on many factors and on using a measure not limited to material gains (MS pp.14-15)
parts.er: Worked well as a discriminator. Three elements were expected: globalisation (more than trade: capital, labour, technology), the characteristics of low-income countries integrated into the argument, and clear links to living standards (e.g. growth -> tax revenue -> health, housing, education). Evaluation often came through MNCs, resource depletion, environmental damage, labour exploitation; a judgement on these could reach AO3 Level 2 (PER 2023-03 pp.10-11).

parts.ask: Case 'Competition, monopoly and the market' (RSA Journal 2020: competition law has not prevented high concentration ratios; mergers approved and monopolies tolerated on the assumption that they are efficient and innovative; the law's 'consumer welfare' test looks only at lower prices; prices ignore negative externalities of production; a low price/low wage spiral; unequal bargaining power of large firms over workers and small suppliers; call for a new competition law). Explain what is meant by a concentration ratio and how it is calculated.
parts.final_form: meaning (combined market share of the n largest firms, 0-100%, lower = more competition) + method (sum of the n largest firms' sales / total industry sales, as a percentage)
parts.ms: 2 meaning: sum of the market shares (%) of the largest specified number of firms, ranging 0-100% and indicating the degree of competition (low ratio = more competition); 2 calculation: add the sales of the n largest firms (e.g. a 4-firm ratio), divide by total industry sales, convert to a percentage (MS p.5)
parts.er: Vague answers: little on what the ratio says about the degree of competition; too many did not go beyond 'adding together total sales of the largest firms' (PER 2023-06 p.21).

parts.ask: Explain, with an example, whether the article is correct in saying that neither the producer nor the consumer pays for negative externalities.
parts.final_form: definition (a cost borne by a third party) + one production-externality example applied to the article's claim
parts.ms: 1 negative externality = a cost incurred by a third party; 1 third parties bear part of the cost of production without any influence over the production decision; 1 relevant example of production affecting a third party + 1 application; max 3 if only a consumption externality (or only the consumer) is discussed (MS p.5)
parts.er: Many argued that a tax would make the externality paid for, and wrote about consumption instead of the effect of production on a third party; surprisingly few gave a relevant example or said a negative externality is a cost incurred by a third party (PER 2023-06 p.21).

parts.ask: Apart from negative externalities, describe two reasons why the article says increased concentration in an industry may not improve consumer welfare.
parts.final_form: two reasons taken from the article, each identified and explained (2 + 2)
parts.ms: 2 per reason (1 identification, 1 explanation): more monopoly power and higher profits benefit shareholders and managers, not consumers; unequal bargaining power between employers and workers, little scope for pay rises; unequal negotiation between large organisations and small independent suppliers forced to accept low purchase prices (e.g. supermarkets and small farmers) (MS p.5)
parts.er: Many did not give two reasons linked to the text and wrote generally about lack of competition; answers that did not follow the wording of the question scored nothing (PER 2023-06 p.21).

parts.ask: The article says monopolies are tolerated because they are efficient. Assess, with the help of a diagram, whether economic theory supports the idea that monopolies are efficient.
parts.final_form: definitions of productive and allocative efficiency + correctly labelled monopoly diagram (MC cutting AC at its minimum) + conclusion that theory does not support the view
parts.ms: 2 productive efficiency = producing at the lowest cost for the output; 2 allocative efficiency = each good produced up to where the marginal benefit of the last unit equals its marginal cost; 3 correctly drawn and labelled monopoly diagram; 1 conclusion: the theory does not support this opinion (MS p.6)
parts.er: Candidates often cited dynamic efficiency and economies of scale; allocative efficiency was less well known than productive. A labelled monopoly diagram was expected and accuracy mattered: the MC curve 'always intersects AC curve at its minimum point', missed by many. 1 mark for the concluding remark, often omitted (PER 2023-06 p.21).

parts.ask: Section B essay: to improve allocative efficiency, economists often advise governments to remove existing subsidies to private-sector providers of education. With the help of a diagram, evaluate this advice.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); subsidy diagram required; ends with a justified judgement on the net benefits of private versus public provision of education
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: public vs private ownership; education as a merit good; links between merit good, positive externalities and allocative efficiency; private provision, subsidies and efficient outcomes; diagram of a subsidy's effect on private provision. Cap: 'Where no diagram – max marks top L2'. AO3: the right level of subsidy is hard to judge; subsidies are costly (opportunity cost); access by ability to pay is inequitable; the profit motive can cut costs and bureaucracy; direct state provision may be less efficient; conclusion weighing private against public provision. The AO3 list also carries generic bullets on negative externalities and advertising that do not fit this question (MS pp.7-8)
parts.er: Least popular micro essay, not well answered: most argued that removing the subsidy raises price and cuts quantity; merit goods, social benefits and the public sector were seldom considered and few analysed the merit good - positive externality - allocative efficiency links; weaker answers did not identify education as a merit good; no relevant diagram meant no Level 3 (PER 2023-06 pp.21-22).

parts.ask: Section B essay: some firms frequently use price discrimination. Assess the view that when this occurs it will always benefit the producer at the expense of the consumer and society.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement: the producer gains (rational profit maximiser) but whether this is always at the expense of consumers and society is debatable
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: conditions for effective price discrimination (power to set price, separable markets with different PED); practical examples; at least one model showing effects on the producer's price, output and profit; effects on consumers' prices and quantities; labelled diagrams useful but not mandatory. AO3: a rational profit maximiser must gain; consumer surplus is transferred to producers; domestic/foreign discrimination may help the balance of payments; some consumers gain and some lose: 'The lower price in the low PED market will benefit those consumers in that market whilst the opposite occurs in the High PED market' (MS wording); extra profit may fund R&D and dynamic efficiency, later lowering prices; conclusion that producer gain is likely but 'at the expense of' consumers/society is debatable (MS pp.9-10)
parts.er: Popular; good balanced answers addressed producer, consumer and society and reached the evaluation marks; weaker answers took price discrimination to mean charging higher prices and ignored its conditions; better ones used practical examples and at least one model, usually third-degree price discrimination; price discrimination diagrams were an opportunity (PER 2023-06 pp.21-22).

parts.ask: Section C essay: an increase in a government's budget surplus will increase unemployment in the short run but make it easier to control a current account deficit on the balance of payments in the long run. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on both halves of the statement (short-run unemployment, long-run current account)
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: budget surplus as government income above expenditure; links from a surplus to AMD and unemployment; the type of unemployment involved; interest-rate links to unemployment in the short run; BoP accounts and how fiscal policy affects them; how a surplus helps control the BoP in the long run. AO3: the short-run effect depends on the cause of existing unemployment and on spare capacity; supply-side policies better if unemployment is structural; a surplus may lower interest rates, e.g. a housing boom, and a fall in rates may make the BoP harder to control; conclusion comparing alternatives and judging the statement (MS pp.11-12)
parts.er: Least popular macro essay; most explained a budget surplus and some linked falling AD to unemployment; BoP effects were poorly applied and many wrongly believed government receives revenue from exports; few analysed the long-run link between a surplus and control of the BoP; AD/AS diagrams were an opportunity (PER 2023-06 pp.21-22).

parts.ask: Section C essay: to what extent do you agree that an increase in productivity will lead to a higher standard of living in low-income countries?
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement on how far higher productivity raises living standards in low-income countries
parts.ms: The MS prints no AO1/AO2 indicative content for this question, only AO3 points, part of them written for an FDI question: technology transfer may raise productivity but substitute capital for labour and raise unemployment; FDI may exploit raw materials and cut long-run growth; government must turn extra wealth into equitable outcomes; living standards also depend on services such as health and education, hard to measure; MNC profits repatriated, skilled jobs kept for expatriates, tax revenue not necessarily invested in health, education, infrastructure; conclusion: productivity has a potential role but the outcome depends on many factors, and the SoL measure should not be purely material (MS pp.13-14)
parts.er: Popular, but production and productivity were often confused and low-income countries were described only as having low GDP; many discussed GDP broadly without clear reference to 'productivity'; good answers saw FDI exploitation, uneven income distribution, health and education provision and the difficulty of measuring the resulting changes (PER 2023-06 pp.21-22).

parts.ask: Case 'Pakistan and the Belt and Roads Initiative (BRI)' (China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, US$50bn; Chinese loans; Pakistan foreign debt about 25% of GDP; Table 1.1 China/Pakistan 2014 vs 2018: GDP per head at PPP 11,917->15,243 and 4,171->4,740; unemployment 4.1->3.8% and 5.8->5.5%; Gini 43.7->38.5 and 29.8->33.5). Explain what is meant by purchasing power parity (PPP).
parts.final_form: definition: cost of the same bundle in local currency compared with another currency (an implied exchange rate)
parts.ms: 1 cost of a bundle of goods and services bought with the local currency; 1 compared with the cost of the same bundle in another currency; e.g. bundle costing 500 rupees and US$2 gives PPP of 250R = $1 (MS p.7)
parts.er: Few understood PPP; a small number knew a bundle was involved but not how it translates into an exchange rate (PER 2023-06 p.23). ECR: even the high answer needed to say the prices of the two baskets are compared to create the exchange rate (ECR p.9).

parts.ask: Explain, with the help of a diagram, the likely impact of the BRI on both the potential and the actual economic growth of Pakistan.
parts.final_form: labelled PPC diagram showing x->y (actual growth) and PPC1->PPC2 (potential growth); AS/AD diagrams also rewarded
parts.ms: 1 actual growth = increase in GDP using existing resources; 1 potential growth = outward movement of the PPC; 1 accurately drawn and labelled graph; 2 showing/referring to x->y for actual and PPC1->PPC2 for potential; max 3 if the diagram is not accurately drawn and labelled (MS p.7)
parts.er: Relatively well answered; PPC or AS/AD diagrams rewarded; some drew correct diagrams but could not explain actual vs potential growth (PER 2023-06 p.23). ECR: label the diagram correctly and use the question's terms; a vague reference to actual growth gained nothing (ECR pp.9, 14).

parts.ask: Consider, with reference to Table 1.1, the change in the standard of living in Pakistan and China between 2014 and 2018.
parts.final_form: define SoL (material and non-material); use the three indicators for both countries (GDP per head +28% China, +14% Pakistan; unemployment down in both; Gini down in China, up in Pakistan); judge; note missing non-material data
parts.ms: 1 meaning of SoL; 1 material vs non-material; data statements 1 each (max 3): GDP per head up 28% China and 14% Pakistan, unemployment fell in both, Gini fell in China and rose in Pakistan; developments 1 each (max 3): both better off materially; income more evenly spread in China, less in Pakistan; material SoL likely up in China, may have fallen in Pakistan; rising employment raises SoL; no data on non-material aspects such as pollution or working hours (MS p.8)
parts.er: Most used the data to show the changes, fewer explained how they affect living standards or defined SoL; the Gini coefficient caused most trouble (whether a rise means more or less equality) (PER 2023-06 p.23). ECR: define SoL, relate each of the three indicators to it, mention non-financial aspects, finish by saying which country's SoL rose most; comparing the two countries instead of tracking change gave the wrong emphasis (ECR pp.9, 11, 14).

parts.ask: Evaluate, using the article, the likely long-run impact of the BRI on the economies of Pakistan and China.
parts.final_form: two-sided answer covering both countries, ending with a judgement based on the evidence
parts.ms: Advantages - China: exports of capital and rail equipment, cement, steel; cheaper routes to Middle East and western markets develop western provinces; uses excess capacity; market for Chinese bank loans. Pakistan: inward investment (railways, port, industrial zones); higher AD and AS; reliable electricity helps industry, households and human capital. Disadvantages: coal/nuclear power polluting; debts to repay (already about 25% of GDP), risk of default; jobs may go to Chinese labour; profitability for Pakistan unclear. Max 5 advantages; max 5 disadvantages; max 5 if one country only; max 7 for two-sided; 1 for the judgement (MS p.9)
parts.er: Most gained 4+ by using the text to show how Pakistan and/or China benefit; the best also recognised limitations (PER 2023-06 p.24). ECR: cover a wider range of advantages and disadvantages rather than a few in depth, and write a stronger conclusion; general Q1 guidance: base answers on the data, develop rather than copy the text, let the marks per part guide length (ECR pp.9, 11, 14).

parts.ask: Section B essay: EVs are encouraged in climate-change policy because they create fewer negative externalities than diesel and petrol vehicles. Evaluate, with the help of diagram(s), two policies a government may use to encourage the use of EVs.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the relative effectiveness of the two chosen policies
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: allocative efficiency (AR = MC or MSB = MSC) and market failure; negative externality where MSC > MPC (or MPB > MSB) -> over-production; intervention options: subsidies to consumers or producers, positive advertising, direct provision of alternative transport, indirect taxation, nudges; labelled externality diagram comparing market and allocatively efficient output with the welfare change, amended for the chosen policy and referred to in the text. AO3: the right subsidy is hard to measure; subsidies have an opportunity cost and need value judgements; effects take time; advertising costly and uncertain; direct provision costly and may be less efficient; the net effect is not always positive and depends on the good (MS pp.10-11)
parts.er: Attempted by a large majority. Strong answers began by explaining how EVs reduce the negative consumption externality compared with diesel or gas vehicles, with a correctly labelled diagram that the answer referred to, and analysed both policies the same way; many reached only Level 1 evaluation, better ones developed it to Level 2 (PER 2023-06 p.24). ECR: define externalities as the gap between private and social costs/benefits, refer to market failure, label every diagram and explain what P1/P2 show (ECR pp.17, 21).

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate, with the help of diagram(s), how total market demand and minimum efficient scale may determine the form of market structure in an industry.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far market size and MES determine the number of firms and so the structure
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: increasing/constant/decreasing returns to scale; MES = output where LRAC is first minimised; economies of scale (division of labour, financial, marketing, managerial, technical) and the LRAC; total demand divided by MES = maximum number of firms at MES; market structures; e.g. MES 50% of the market -> duopoly, 2% -> about 50 firms; LRAC diagram marking MES and demand. AO3: MES changes over time (technology); how the market is defined matters (village shop); niche small-scale high-cost producers survive (luxury cars, designer clothes) (MS p.12)
parts.er: Very few attempted it and most had only partly read the question: some covered economies of scale and MES against demand but did not go on to market structure; others wrote all they knew about market structures with no reference to demand or MES (PER 2023-06 p.24). ECR: pick out 'total market', 'minimum efficient scale' and 'market structure'; argue that a market of size X with MES Y supports Q firms, name the resulting structure, then evaluate its realism (ECR pp.24, 27).

parts.ask: Section C essay: consider the extent to which depreciation of its exchange rate contributes to the economic growth of a low-income country.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the extent of the contribution for a low-income country
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: effect of depreciation on the currency's external value; prices of exports and imports and their demand; (X - M) and AD; injections/leakages, multiplier or 45-degree diagram; AD/AS diagram for national income; explicit link to actual or potential growth. AO3: whether supply capacity can respond; agricultural exports price-inelastic in supply compared with oil; short-run gain in employment but inflation; debt servicing helped if debt is in domestic currency, harmed if in foreign currency (MS p.13)
parts.er: Good answers analysed exports and imports and then GDP through AS/AD, and evaluated outcomes for a low-income country; weaker answers dealt only with the depreciation and ignored the low-income country and evaluation (PER 2023-06 p.24). ECR: make explicit, developed reference to a low-income country; develop the ideas through AS/AD and the AD equation to show how (X - M) affects demand; draw clearer diagrams (ECR pp.32, 35, 37).

parts.ask: Section C essay: evaluate the effectiveness of using monetary policy to reduce inflation and how this policy may affect a government's ability to achieve its other macroeconomic aims.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on effectiveness against inflation and the conflicts with other aims
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: monetary tools (interest rate, money supply, exchange rate, reserve asset ratio); define inflation and the other aims (low unemployment, growth, balance of payments equilibrium); higher interest rates cut consumer demand and investment (transmission mechanism or AS/AD); apply the model to the other aims; Phillips curve trade-off. AO3: accuracy of the required rate/ratio change; time lags; expectations; explicit comment on whether each other aim is still met; two examples of conflict; short- vs long-run effects on growth; rational-expectations critique of the Phillips curve; exchange rate, BoP and Marshall-Lerner (MS pp.14-15)
parts.er: Better answers analysed contractionary monetary policy through AS/AD or the Keynesian 45-degree diagram, effects on consumption and investment, and several instruments (rates, reserve asset ratio, quantitative tightening), then its effects on the other aims; weaker answers wrote about expansionary policy and rising inflation, were descriptive, or ignored the other aims (PER 2023-06 p.24). ECR: analyse the transmission mechanism; refer to both diagrams in the text; give relevant evaluation (ECR pp.39, 43, 46).

parts.ask: Case 'Competition, monopoly and the market' (RSA Journal 2020: competition law has not prevented high concentration ratios; mergers approved and monopolies tolerated on the assumption that they are efficient and innovative; the law's 'consumer welfare' test looks only at lower prices; prices ignore negative externalities of production; a low price/low wage spiral; unequal bargaining power of large firms over workers and small suppliers; call for a new competition law). Explain what is meant by a concentration ratio and how it is calculated.
parts.final_form: meaning (combined market share of the n largest firms, 0-100%, lower = more competition) + method (sum of the n largest firms' sales / total industry sales, as a percentage)
parts.ms: 2 meaning: sum of the market shares (%) of the largest specified number of firms, ranging 0-100% and indicating the degree of competition (low ratio = more competition); 2 calculation: add the sales of the n largest firms (e.g. a 4-firm ratio), divide by total industry sales, convert to a percentage (MS p.5)
parts.er: Vague answers: little on what the ratio says about the degree of competition; too many did not go beyond 'adding together total sales of the largest firms' (PER 2023-06 p.25). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Explain, with an example, whether the article is correct in saying that neither the producer nor the consumer pays for negative externalities.
parts.final_form: definition (a cost borne by a third party) + one production-externality example applied to the article's claim
parts.ms: 1 negative externality = a cost incurred by a third party; 1 third parties bear part of the cost of production without any influence over the production decision; 1 relevant example of production affecting a third party + 1 application; max 3 if only a consumption externality (or only the consumer) is discussed (MS p.5)
parts.er: Many argued that a tax would make the externality paid for, and wrote about consumption instead of the effect of production on a third party; surprisingly few gave a relevant example or said a negative externality is a cost incurred by a third party (PER 2023-06 p.25). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Apart from negative externalities, describe two reasons why the article says increased concentration in an industry may not improve consumer welfare.
parts.final_form: two reasons taken from the article, each identified and explained (2 + 2)
parts.ms: 2 per reason (1 identification, 1 explanation): more monopoly power and higher profits benefit shareholders and managers, not consumers; unequal bargaining power between employers and workers, little scope for pay rises; unequal negotiation between large organisations and small independent suppliers forced to accept low purchase prices (e.g. supermarkets and small farmers) (MS p.5)
parts.er: Many did not give two reasons linked to the text and wrote generally about lack of competition; answers that did not follow the wording of the question scored nothing (PER 2023-06 p.25). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: The article says monopolies are tolerated because they are efficient. Assess, with the help of a diagram, whether economic theory supports the idea that monopolies are efficient.
parts.final_form: definitions of productive and allocative efficiency + correctly labelled monopoly diagram (MC cutting AC at its minimum) + conclusion that theory does not support the view
parts.ms: 2 productive efficiency = producing at the lowest cost for the output; 2 allocative efficiency = each good produced up to where the marginal benefit of the last unit equals its marginal cost; 3 correctly drawn and labelled monopoly diagram; 1 conclusion: the theory does not support this opinion (MS p.6)
parts.er: Candidates often cited dynamic efficiency and economies of scale; allocative efficiency was less well known than productive. A labelled monopoly diagram was expected and accuracy mattered: the MC curve 'always intersects AC curve at its minimum point', missed by many. 1 mark for the concluding remark, often omitted (PER 2023-06 p.25). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section B essay: to improve allocative efficiency, economists often advise governments to remove existing subsidies to private-sector providers of education. With the help of a diagram, evaluate this advice.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); subsidy diagram required; ends with a justified judgement on the net benefits of private versus public provision of education
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: public vs private ownership; education as a merit good; links between merit good, positive externalities and allocative efficiency; private provision, subsidies and efficient outcomes; diagram of a subsidy's effect on private provision. Cap: 'Where no diagram – max marks top L2'. AO3: the right level of subsidy is hard to judge; subsidies are costly (opportunity cost); access by ability to pay is inequitable; the profit motive can cut costs and bureaucracy; direct state provision may be less efficient; conclusion weighing private against public provision. The AO3 list also carries generic bullets on negative externalities and advertising that do not fit this question (MS pp.7-8)
parts.er: Least popular micro essay, not well answered: most argued that removing the subsidy raises price and cuts quantity; merit goods, social benefits and the public sector were seldom considered and few analysed the merit good - positive externality - allocative efficiency links; weaker answers did not identify education as a merit good; no relevant diagram meant no Level 3 (PER 2023-06 pp.25-26). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section B essay: some firms frequently use price discrimination. Assess the view that when this occurs it will always benefit the producer at the expense of the consumer and society.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement: the producer gains (rational profit maximiser) but whether this is always at the expense of consumers and society is debatable
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: conditions for effective price discrimination (power to set price, separable markets with different PED); practical examples; at least one model showing effects on the producer's price, output and profit; effects on consumers' prices and quantities; labelled diagrams useful but not mandatory. AO3: a rational profit maximiser must gain; consumer surplus is transferred to producers; domestic/foreign discrimination may help the balance of payments; some consumers gain and some lose: 'The lower price in the low PED market will benefit those consumers in that market whilst the opposite occurs in the High PED market' (MS wording); extra profit may fund R&D and dynamic efficiency, later lowering prices; conclusion that producer gain is likely but 'at the expense of' consumers/society is debatable (MS pp.9-10)
parts.er: Popular; good balanced answers addressed producer, consumer and society and reached the evaluation marks; weaker answers took price discrimination to mean charging higher prices and ignored its conditions; better ones used practical examples and at least one model, usually third-degree price discrimination; price discrimination diagrams were an opportunity (PER 2023-06 pp.25-26). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section C essay: an increase in a government's budget surplus will increase unemployment in the short run but make it easier to control a current account deficit on the balance of payments in the long run. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on both halves of the statement (short-run unemployment, long-run current account)
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: budget surplus as government income above expenditure; links from a surplus to AMD and unemployment; the type of unemployment involved; interest-rate links to unemployment in the short run; BoP accounts and how fiscal policy affects them; how a surplus helps control the BoP in the long run. AO3: the short-run effect depends on the cause of existing unemployment and on spare capacity; supply-side policies better if unemployment is structural; a surplus may lower interest rates, e.g. a housing boom, and a fall in rates may make the BoP harder to control; conclusion comparing alternatives and judging the statement (MS pp.11-12)
parts.er: Least popular macro essay; most explained a budget surplus and some linked falling AD to unemployment; BoP effects were poorly applied and many wrongly believed government receives revenue from exports; few analysed the long-run link between a surplus and control of the BoP; AD/AS diagrams were an opportunity (PER 2023-06 pp.25-26). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section C essay: to what extent do you agree that an increase in productivity will lead to a higher standard of living in low-income countries?
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement on how far higher productivity raises living standards in low-income countries
parts.ms: The MS prints no AO1/AO2 indicative content for this question, only AO3 points, part of them written for an FDI question: technology transfer may raise productivity but substitute capital for labour and raise unemployment; FDI may exploit raw materials and cut long-run growth; government must turn extra wealth into equitable outcomes; living standards also depend on services such as health and education, hard to measure; MNC profits repatriated, skilled jobs kept for expatriates, tax revenue not necessarily invested in health, education, infrastructure; conclusion: productivity has a potential role but the outcome depends on many factors, and the SoL measure should not be purely material (MS pp.13-14)
parts.er: Popular, but production and productivity were often confused and low-income countries were described only as having low GDP; many discussed GDP broadly without clear reference to 'productivity'; good answers saw FDI exploitation, uneven income distribution, health and education provision and the difficulty of measuring the resulting changes (PER 2023-06 pp.25-26). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Case 'Economic decline in 2020' (Japan: third quarterly fall in GDP in a row, real GDP lowest since 2011 after 20 years of deflation and stagnation; earlier sales-tax rise, COVID-19 and the US-China trade war, 19.9% of exports to the US and 19% to China; Table 1.1 for 2016/2017/2018/2019: central bank rate 0.1% every year; change in industrial production 0.0/3.1/1.1/0.1%; change in retail sales 0.6/1.9/1.7/0.1%; national debt 236/234/236/237% of GDP; growth 0.5/2.2/0.3/0.7%; IMF: worst global recession since the 1930s; Japan's GDP -7.8% in Apr-Jun 2020 (US -9.5%, China -3.2%); trade deficit US$15.2bn in 2019, almost 50% up on 2018; exports -18.5% in Q3 2020, led by cars; expansionary fiscal and monetary policy, low interest rates since 2016). With reference to Table 1.1, what indicates that Japan's government had borrowed substantially?
parts.final_form: the table statistic quoted: national debt more than twice GDP since 2016
parts.ms: 1 public debt since 2016; 1 more than twice the size of GDP (MS p.8)
parts.er: Full marks needed a reference to Table 1.1: national debt (per cent of GDP) more than twice the size of GDP (PER 2023-11 p.23).

parts.ask: Although Japan was the world's fourth largest exporter, it had suffered trade deficits. Explain how this might have happened.
parts.final_form: two reasons, each identified and developed (2 x 2)
parts.ms: 1 identification + 1 development per reason (2 x 2): value of imports exceeded value of exports, perhaps because of different price elasticities of exports and imports; loss of export sales, seen in falling industrial production (e.g. cars); US-China tensions affecting their trading partners (19% of exports to each) and lower world trade volumes caused by the virus (2); any other relevant reason (MS p.8)
parts.er: Reasonably well answered, but many identified a cause without explaining it; listing four causes alone gained only 2 marks (PER 2023-11 p.23).

parts.ask: Consider whether the evidence provided shows that Japan's economic decline in 2020 was caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
parts.final_form: evidence for (pandemic, IMF figures, lockdown) and against (long-term decline, sales tax), with a judgement on whether the evidence is sufficient
parts.ms: 1 the 2020 decline was exaggerated by the coronavirus; 1 IMF figures on the global economy; 1 the 2020 lockdown cut domestic consumption and exports of goods such as cars; 2 but it was part of a much longer decline: quote the table, two decades of deflation and stagnation before 2011; 1 the 2019 sales tax helps explain falling retail sales (MS p.8)
parts.er: Many did not consider the evidence provided (IMF figures, 2020 lockdown, sales tax); few commented on the sufficiency of the evidence; some missed that the decline was part of a much longer-term decline (two decades of deflation and stagnation before 2011) (PER 2023-11 p.23).

parts.ask: Japan's central bank has kept interest rates low since 2016. Analyse how low rates can stimulate an economy, then evaluate whether they have succeeded in stimulating Japan's economy over that period.
parts.final_form: up to 4 for theory (transmission to consumption and investment; AD/AS diagram accepted) + up to 4 for evaluation using Table 1.1 (best year 2017; retail sales and industrial production weak after it)
parts.ms: Up to 4 theory, up to 4 application of data: low rates encourage consumers and investors to borrow and take risks (2); should discourage saving and raise consumption, but the retail-sales pattern contradicts this (2); should encourage borrowing for investment, but industrial production fell sharply after 2017 (2); policy worked best in 2017 (highest growth, production and retail sales up); falling exports, the US-China trade war and high public debt kept the economy stagnant, made worse by the 2020 pandemic (2) (MS p.9)
parts.er: Most explained that low rates boost the economy by encouraging consumers and investors to borrow; some used AD/AS diagrams; this theory was worth up to 4 marks. Full marks required evaluative comment with reference to the data, which was not done well (PER 2023-11 p.23).

parts.ask: Section B essay: the provision of health care by the public sector is inefficient and therefore all health care should be provided by firms in the private sector. Evaluate this comment.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); evaluation needed even though not asked for in so many words; ends with a justified judgement on the net benefits of public versus private provision
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: public vs private ownership; health care as a merit good; links between merit good, positive externalities and allocative efficiency; public provision and efficient outcomes; causes of inefficiency in public provision. AO3: private providers ignore positive externalities so are unlikely to provide an allocatively efficient level; profit maximisation may raise the cost of care; access by ability to pay is inequitable; the profit motive may cut costs and bureaucracy; private provision may free public resources; conclusion weighing the net benefits of each. The AO3 list also carries generic bullets on negative externalities and advertising (MS pp.10-11)
parts.er: Popular. Better answers distinguished private and public ownership, identified health care as a merit good and referred to positive externalities and allocative efficiency; weaker ones wrote about health care in general terms without economic concepts; few gave Level 2 evaluation. Positive-externality diagrams were an opportunity (PER 2023-11 pp.23-24).

parts.ask: Section B essay: two large firms in the same industry merge with government approval. With the help of a diagram, evaluate the view that the government should have blocked the merger.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); monopoly diagram required; ends with a judgement on whether, on balance, the merger should proceed
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: horizontal integration (same stage of production); likely to create a monopoly; a dominant firm can raise prices and drive out smaller firms (diagram); less choice; X-inefficiency; possible harm to the local labour market. Cap: 'Limit of Level 2 if no relevant diagram'. AO3: larger size may widen consumer choice; dynamic efficiency and long-run investment may lower prices; economies of scale (e.g. managerial) may lower prices; regulation can handle harmful effects when the merger happens; conclusion on whether, on balance, it should proceed (MS p.12)
parts.er: Not popular. Answers identifying the merger as horizontal integration likely to lead to monopoly, and those with a monopoly diagram, scored higher; many gave no relevant or no correctly labelled diagram; better answers argued for and against the increase in size and concluded (PER 2023-11 pp.23-24).

parts.ask: Section C essay: assess the extent to which monetary policy can be used effectively to solve the problem of unemployment.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement comparing monetary policy with fiscal or supply-side alternatives for the type(s) of unemployment
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: monetary instruments (interest rates, money supply, exchange rates); problems of unemployment (inefficient use of resources); causes of unemployment; links from interest rates, money supply or exchange rates to unemployment. AO3: effectiveness depends on the cause, monetary policy acting on AMD works best on cyclical unemployment; some instruments harm other aims (lower rates may depreciate the currency and cause cost-push or demand-pull inflation); supply-side policies better for structural unemployment; low rates may cause a housing boom; conclusion comparing monetary policy with fiscal or supply-side policy (MS p.13)
parts.er: Popular. Good answers knew interest-rate, money-supply and exchange-rate instruments; reference to the types of unemployment was expected; effectiveness was less developed, though better answers saw monetary policy as effective for cyclical unemployment; alternatives were seldom mentioned but some gained evaluation credit by comparing them in the conclusion (PER 2023-11 p.24).

parts.ask: Section C essay: to what extent do you agree with the view that globalisation benefits high-income countries at the expense of low-income countries?
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a balanced judgement (globalisation can benefit both, depending on several factors)
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: globalisation (free trade, free movement of capital and labour, technology transfer, cultural and political ties); characteristics of low-income countries (low productivity, high dependency ratios, low GDP per head, primary exports); high-income countries gain access to goods, health care and education; comparative advantage gives them cheap raw materials; dependency and trade imbalances may hurt low-income countries in the long run. AO3: the links are unclear: technology transfer and skilled labour may help low-income countries; more real wealth can fund merit goods; local firms may reach large markets; conclusion that globalisation can benefit both. Inside Q5 the MS also prints indicative content for a different question on FDI and living standards (MS pp.14-15)
parts.er: Not popular. Candidates linked globalisation to free trade, but few outlined the characteristics of low- and high-income countries (often only one); a balanced conclusion was expected that globalisation can benefit both groups depending on several factors; better answers addressed 'to what extent do you agree' (PER 2023-11 p.24).

parts.ask: Case 'Traffic Control' (2020: Lagos banned motorcycle taxis and tricycles from its most congested areas; the rest of the article is removed from the published QP; the parts and MS show it compared Singapore's car quota system with Electronic Road Pricing (ERP)). Explain what is meant by equity and how the ban affects equity for commuters in Lagos.
parts.final_form: definition (fairness) + application: poorer workers are hit hardest
parts.ms: 1 equity = fairness / fairly treated / justice / people in the same situation get the same treatment; 1 poorer workers rely most on motorcycles and tricycles; 1 poorer workers have to walk long distances in the heat (MS p.8)
parts.er: Overall low marks: some 50 per cent did not know equity means fairness, and many ignored that it was the poorer workers who suffered from the ban (PER 2023-11 p.25).

parts.ask: Explain, with the help of a diagram, what is meant by a negative externality and identify two negative externalities from the article.
parts.final_form: definition + labelled private/social cost-benefit diagram showing over-consumption + two examples from the article
parts.ms: 1 definition: negative spill-over / third-party effect of a private transaction; 1 correctly labelled axes; 1 private/social costs and benefits; 1 explanation that the diagram shows over-consumption; 2x1 examples: deaths, impact on the environment, congestion (MS p.8)
parts.er: Most scored well: a clear definition, a correctly drawn and labelled diagram and two examples from the article (PER 2023-11 p.25).

parts.ask: From the evidence, consider whether Singapore's car quota system or its ERP was more effective in solving traffic congestion.
parts.final_form: evidence on each scheme from the article, then one verdict (the evidence favours ERP)
parts.ms: Quota raised the price/cost of cars 1 but encouraged owners to use their cars more 1, increasing congestion 1; ERP flexible to road conditions 1, varies by time of day 1 and level of congestion 1, motorists rethink time/route/mode of travel 1; max 5; evidence suggests ERP more effective 1 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Answered well using evidence from the article; candidates who said both schemes had merits did not score the final mark. The paper relied on the article more than usual, so close reading paid off (PER 2023-11 p.25).

parts.ask: Assess whether government involvement in providing transport systems is because transport is a public good.
parts.final_form: define a public good by its two characteristics, apply them to transport (tickets, limited capacity), conclude transport is not a public good
parts.ms: 1 non-excludable; 1 non-rival; 1 travel needs a ticket/payment; 1 trains etc. have a given capacity; 1 therefore transport is not a public good (MS p.8)
parts.er: Some knew the two defining characteristics but could not apply them to transport; others applied non-rivalry and non-excludability to public transport and correctly concluded it is not a public good (PER 2023-11 p.25).

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate the use of indifference curve analysis to derive the demand curve for a normal good and the demand curve for an inferior good.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how useful IC analysis is for deriving these demand curves
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: IC assumptions (rational consumers preferring more, two goods, constant prices, substitutability, transitivity, perfect knowledge); IC definition, convexity, IC map; budget line and income changes; substitution and income effects of a price change; positive vs negative income effect gives normal vs inferior good; tangency of IC and budget line as the optimum. AO3: consumer rationality doubtful; a price fall raises demand for both normal and inferior (non-Giffen) goods, so the analysis cannot tell which a good is; durables are one-off indivisible purchases; real consumers buy many goods; static model, preferences change. MS labels the question 2(a) although the QP has no parts (MS pp.9-10)
parts.er: Good answers used clear labelled diagrams separating income and substitution effects and extended this to the demand curve. First winter session with six explicit AO3 marks: strong answers evaluated the assumptions (rational consumer); weaker answers listed or ignored evaluation. Answers based mainly on marginal utility theory instead of IC analysis were restricted to Level 1 (PER 2023-11 p.26).

parts.ask: Section B essay: perfect competition is the ideal form of market structure because it is the most efficient. With the help of diagrams, evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether perfect competition is 'ideal' and 'most efficient'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: productive and allocative efficiency with diagrams; short run and long run; assumptions of perfect competition (many participants, free entry and exit); how they lead to equilibrium and to productive and allocative efficiency; diagrams of short-run profits and the long-run return to normal profit. AO3: realism of the model; perfect competition as a benchmark; comparison with other structures; few real-world examples; monopoly profits can fund R&D and dynamic efficiency (MS p.11)
parts.er: Best answers analysed disequilibrium resolving to equilibrium, applied productive and allocative efficiency at each stage, with clearly labelled diagrams referred to in the essay; evaluation compared another market structure, a few citing dynamic efficiency of oligopoly or monopoly. Weaker answers skipped non-equilibrium positions or types of efficiency; the weakest did not evaluate (PER 2023-11 p.26).

parts.ask: Section C essay: the presence of multinational corporations (MNCs) in a low-income country always promotes economic growth there. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether MNC presence 'always' promotes growth
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: transfer of managerial and workshop skills; larger tax base for government investment; define MNC and actual (short-term) vs potential (long-term) growth; FDI effects on AS/PPF via the multiplier, circular flow or AD/AS; better education and health for long-term growth. AO3: MNCs evade home-country rules (export 'dirty' industry and its negative externalities, weaker labour and safety laws); destroy local industry, net job loss; local monopoly with higher prices and lower output; transfer pricing to tax havens; effects on macro aims; low-skilled local jobs with expatriates in senior roles (MS p.12)
parts.er: Highest response rate. Good answers defined MNC, low-income country and economic growth, then analysed the MNC's effect on aggregate demand (actual growth, AS/AD or Keynesian) and on capacity (potential growth via education, health or resources); good evaluation on exploitative behaviour; some wrote about the standard of living instead of growth (PER 2023-11 p.26).

parts.ask: Section C essay: consider the relative merits of gross national income (GNI) and the multidimensional poverty index (MPI) as measures of the standard of living.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on which measure (or which combination) better captures the standard of living
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: GNI = income earned in the country plus net receipts from abroad, a money aggregate, boosted by remittances and overseas investment income; MPI definition and weights: health 1/3 (child mortality, nutrition), education 1/3 (years of schooling, attendance), living standards 1/3 (cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets, 1/18 each); GNI measures money values, MPI the adequacy of essential goods and services. AO3: GNI must be deflated and divided by population; hidden and illegal activity; income from externality-causing or monopoly activity counts; no distribution measure (Gini needed); MPI data harder to collect; income-poor and multidimensionally poor groups only partly overlap, so both are needed; growth does not always reduce deprivation; GNI data for 188 countries, MPI for 103; MPI education counts inputs not outputs (MS pp.13-14)
parts.er: Lowest response rate. Those who explained the standard of living and judged how well GNI and MPI fit it scored well; others paid little attention to the standard of living, wrote about GDP alone, or ignored the MPI (PER 2023-11 p.26).

parts.ask: Case 'The decline of South Africa's economy' (most industrialised African economy but highly unequal; reforms to redistribute income undermined by poor management of state railways, ports, airways and electricity; GDP -3.2% in Q1 2020, the biggest quarterly fall in a decade; GDP per head US$6130 in Dec 2019, 5.8% below Dec 2018; the state-owned electricity monopoly rationed power with regular cuts, its debts adding to a national debt of 56% of GDP, called the biggest threat; a mining ownership reform made firms, including MNCs, stop investing; weak education, skills shortage, unemployment up to 27%; restrictive union practices; analyst: lack of private investment and FDI, due to policy, uncertainty and mismanagement, is a critical reason for low growth. Figures read approximately from a 110 dpi render: Fig. 1.1 annual growth 2008-2019, about 3% in 2008, about -1.5% in 2009, about 3% in 2010-11, drifting down to about 0.5% in 2016, about 1.5% in 2017 and 1% in 2018, about -3% at the end; Fig. 1.2 unemployment rate 2009-2019, fluctuating upward from about 23.5% to about 27.5%; Fig. 1.3 FDI net inflows, about 3.5% of GDP in 2008, about 1% in 2010-11, about 2.2% in 2013, about 0.5% in 2015, about 1.5% in 2018). Describe what is meant by economic equality and distinguish it from equity.
parts.final_form: two contrasted definitions: equality = equal distribution; equity = fairness
parts.ms: 2 economic equality = equal distribution of income, wealth and opportunities across society (affecting job prospects, earnings, education); 2 equity = fairness/justice/any relevant comment; max 3 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Well prepared: the overwhelming majority gained at least 2 of the 3 marks (PER 2023-11 p.27).

parts.ask: Define actual economic growth and analyse the relationship between economic growth and unemployment as illustrated by Fig. 1.1 and Fig. 1.2.
parts.final_form: definition (% change in real GDP over a period, 2 marks) + trend-based analysis (inverse relationship; falling growth trend with rising unemployment trend)
parts.ms: actual growth = % change in a country's real national output (GDP) (1) in a period of time (1); 'employment fluctuates but there is a general rising trend' (1, MS wording); falling growth goes with rising unemployment, an inverse relationship (1); negative growth matches the highest unemployment (1); the general growth trend is falling (1); max 5 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Most gained both definition marks (an increase in real GDP over a period); many lost marks on the relationship by reading off values at single dates instead of using the long-term trends in growth and unemployment (PER 2023-11 p.27).

parts.ask: Assess the article's evidence on how far the performance of the state-owned electricity monopoly contributed to South Africa's economic decline.
parts.final_form: evidence on the company's effect weighed against other causes, ending with a conclusion (exact significance cannot be determined)
parts.ms: 1 electricity is fundamental; demand not met, power cuts ration use; 1 other industries also declining but the article calls the company the biggest threat; 1 power shortages cut mining and manufacturing output, raising unemployment; 1 general uncertainty reduced investment, keeping actual growth well below potential despite natural resources; 1 no comparable figures for other industries, so no definite conclusion on its exact significance; 1 its debts add significantly to the national debt; max 5 (MS p.8)
parts.er: The least well answered part. 'Assess' meant searching the article for evidence of significance; many noted power cuts without explaining why they mattered; the strongest saw the importance of 'general uncertainty'; a conclusion based on the evidence earned an additional mark and was often missing (PER 2023-11 pp.27-28).

parts.ask: Evaluate whether attracting investment and managing uncertainty are the most effective ways to improve the prospects for South Africa's economy.
parts.final_form: argument using the evidence on investment and uncertainty, short run vs long run, other measures (skills, union practices, infrastructure), and a judgement
parts.ms: 1 each: reforms and poor state industries undermined confidence; no private investment in mining, so rising unemployment; FDI fell (Fig. 1.3); high unemployment means low spending and slow AD growth; limited prospects in the short run; long run needs education reform for skills and reform of restrictive union practices; but some recent rise in FDI; long-term infrastructure investment; rise in employment/growth; max 7 (MS p.9)
parts.er: Answered successfully overall. The focus had to be on attracting investment and managing uncertainty: an argument on how effectively these could be achieved and a judgement based on the evidence; future prospects, a short-run/long-run distinction, the skills shortage and more FDI were expected (PER 2023-11 p.28).

parts.ask: Section B essay: pollution is caused when consumers or producers make decisions based on self-interest, a sign of market failure. With the help of a diagram, evaluate the extent to which government policies should rely on market forces to address this market failure.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); externality diagram required; ends with a judgement on how far policy should rely on market forces rather than direct intervention
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: link between pollution and market failure; pollution from production or consumption; negative externalities; diagram linking negative externalities and market failure; how market forces can address it. AO3: profit-maximising firms ignore social cost; the right tax is hard to measure; minimum prices only partly effective and hit profits and employment; non-price measures such as a complete ban may control externalities more precisely; effects take time; advertising costly and uncertain; conclusion weighing direct intervention against market-based policies (MS pp.10-11)
parts.er: Very popular and well prepared. A diagram was essential; a production or a consumption externality diagram was accepted if accurately labelled and used. Strong answers identified policies and judged how far policy should rely on market forces; weaker ones gave a brief evaluative statement; at least 4/6 was possible for a fully developed conclusion (PER 2023-11 p.28).

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate the view that monopolistically competitive firms will always charge lower prices and operate more efficiently than a monopoly firm.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a conclusion addressing both price and efficiency for both structures and testing 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: characteristics of monopolistic competition; short-run vs long-run profit-maximising output; monopoly characteristics and the key difference (barriers to entry); types of efficiency; links between monopoly, higher prices and inefficiency, compared with monopolistic competition in the short and long run. AO3: monopoly R&D and dynamic efficiency may lower costs and prices; monopoly economies of scale may lower prices; non-price competition adds costs in monopolistic competition; 'Monopolistically competitive firms will achieve productive efficiency in the long run but a profit maximizing firm will not operate at an allocatively efficient level of output' (MS wording); conclusion on both price and efficiency and the word 'always' (MS p.12)
parts.er: Fewer attempted it. Most knew both structures; adding short- and long-run profit-maximising output gave lower Level 2, and relative prices and efficiency in both runs moved answers into Level 3. 'Always' was the key word: strong answers showed when a monopoly might charge less (economies of scale, dynamic efficiency); the highest marks covered both price and efficiency (PER 2023-11 p.28).

parts.ask: Section C essay: with the help of a diagram, assess the effectiveness of using fiscal policy to close a negative output gap in an economy.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); diagram of the gap required; ends with a judgement on effectiveness against side effects and alternatives
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: fiscal policy (taxation and spending to influence macro goals); output gap = actual minus potential output; a negative gap means spare capacity from too little AMD, shown on a diagram; higher spending or lower taxes raise AD; a budget deficit's injection has a multiplied effect on output, income and employment. AO3: a larger deficit may raise interest rates and crowd out the private sector; the size of the gap is hard to forecast; a money-financed deficit may cause long-run inflation; supply-side policies may close the gap without inflation risk; more imports may harm the BoP. The rest of the AO3 list is about devaluation and seems to belong to another question (MS pp.13-14)
parts.er: About half chose it; a more technical question needing a clear grasp of fiscal policy and of a negative output gap (the term, rather than 'deflationary gap', may have deterred some). Analysis was well done; a relevant diagram was essential; the strongest added the multiplier; evaluation credit for crowding out, the difficulty of forecasting the gap, and supply-side alternatives in the long run (PER 2023-11 pp.28-29).

parts.ask: Section C essay: assess the impact of international aid on the standard of living in low-income countries.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement on the short- and long-term effect of different types of aid on living standards
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: aid = assistance not provided through normal market forces; humanitarian vs development aid (long-term loans, tied, bilateral, multilateral); characteristics of low-income countries; low living standards (poverty, inequality, poor housing, education and health, rapid population growth); aid for technology, factories and training raises productivity, output, employment and income; more real wealth and tax revenue for health, housing and education. AO3: the aid-living standards link is unclear (corruption, reaches few); types differ: loans may deepen the cycle of poverty; aid given for political reasons; tied aid forces dearer purchases from the donor; dependency reduces innovation; conclusion on the short- and long-term efficacy of development aid (MS pp.15-16)
parts.er: Part of a rarely tested syllabus section. Low-income characteristics and the link to living standards were generally understood, but the types of aid much less so; few went beyond describing aid in general, which kept answers at Level 2 for lack of analysis; evaluation was expected on why different types of aid have different effects (PER 2023-11 p.29).

parts.ask: Case 'French electricity prices' (2022: government ordered a partly state-owned company to sell more electricity cheaply and to rivals at a 40% discount; tax cut to hold household price rises to 4% instead of an expected 35%; global gas shortage; 18 of 56 nuclear plants closed; UK rise expected 56%). Identify what caused the price rise and explain whether the article shows it was an example of market failure.
parts.final_form: two causes + definition of market failure + verdict (no evidence of allocative inefficiency, so no market failure; either verdict accepted)
parts.ms: 1 natural gas supply shortage; 1 breakdown of nuclear reactors; 2 market failure = price mechanism fails to account for all costs and benefits, giving allocative inefficiency (alternative definitions accepted); 1 no evidence of allocative inefficiency, so no market failure (accept either) (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Is there any evidence in the article that the French government's decisions will increase competition or efficiency in the energy market?
parts.final_form: evidence points for each, then a conclusion: some evidence of more competition, none of more efficiency
parts.ms: 1 competitors got cheaper electricity, so maybe more competition; 1 renewable projects stopped, possibly less efficiency; 1 five reactors closed through poor maintenance, less efficient (self-sufficiency now less likely); 1 conclusion: some evidence of more competition, none of more efficiency; 1 accept: lower monopoly profit may cut dynamic efficiency; max 4 (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Distinguish between equality and equity.
parts.final_form: two definitions, at least one developed
parts.ms: 1 equality = equal distribution of income/wealth in society + 1 development; 1 equity = fairness/justice, especially in welfare economics + 1 development; max 3 (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Consider whether the French government's actions on electricity prices might be thought to increase either equality or equity for consumers and producers.
parts.final_form: separate, qualified verdicts on equality and equity for consumers and for producers
parts.ms: Price changes cannot be linked to fairness for the producer 1, so producer equity unaffected 1; tax cut might raise consumer equity 1; explanation 1; consumer equality possibly up, rescued from excessive price rises 1, but rich and poor both benefit so not conclusive 1; small firms get cheaper electricity at the large firm's expense, so producer equality may rise 2; but the tax cut may help the large company more than its rivals, so the producer equality effect is uncertain 2; max 8 (MS p.9)

parts.ask: Section B essay: with the help of a diagram, assess the effectiveness of a government's intervention in the price mechanism to address the causes of climate change.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the net benefits of price-based intervention compared with direct controls
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: link between climate change and negative externalities; externalities of production or consumption; diagram of the link; how market forces can address the consequences. L2 maximum if no accurate diagram. AO3: the climate-externality link is hard to establish and externalities hard to measure; the correct tax is hard to set, so tax will not remove all externalities; minimum prices only partly effective and hit profits and jobs; non-price measures (an outright ban) may control more precisely; conclusion weighing direct intervention against market forces (MS pp.10-11)

parts.ask: Section B essay: introducing a trade union into a perfectly competitive labour market will always lead to higher wages and higher unemployment. With the help of a diagram, evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on each element of the statement and the word 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: characteristics of a perfectly competitive labour market; role and aims of a trade union (wage bargaining); diagram of wage determination and its effect on each firm's wage and employment; ways a union might affect wages and employment through supply of and demand for labour; extent of union influence. L2 maximum if no accurate diagram. AO3: unions may raise productivity through training (though capital substitution may cut jobs); higher wages make capital relatively cheaper; effect depends on ease of capital-labour substitution and existing capital intensity; a wage above equilibrium creates excess supply of labour, size set by elasticities of labour supply and demand; conclusion addressing each element and 'always' (MS pp.12-13)

parts.ask: Section C essay: with the help of a diagram, assess the effectiveness of government policies which might be used to reduce cost-push inflation.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on which approach is most effective in the short run and in the long run
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: causes of inflation and why it is a problem; cost-push causes with an accurately labelled diagram; policies: long run raise AS through productivity (education, infrastructure), short run cut costs (widespread subsidies, lower indirect taxes, removing tariffs on key imports, incomes policies). L2 maximum if no accurate diagram; must refer to some supply-side policies for L3. AO3: subsidies/tax cuts worsen the budget and raise borrowing; removing tariffs hurts domestic producers and jobs; incomes policies face union opposition; productivity investment may raise short-run unemployment; training is costly; infrastructure spending adds to AD and inflation at first; compare short- and long-run effectiveness; evaluation of demand-side policies accepted (MS pp.14-15)

parts.ask: Section C essay: globalisation will help high-income economies achieve economic growth and this will automatically improve living standards. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on short- and long-term benefits and whether the improvement is 'automatic'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: globalisation (free trade, movement of capital and labour, technology transfer, cultural and political ties); high-income country characteristics (high productivity, high GDP per head, secondary/tertiary exports); signs of high living standards (low poverty, advanced infrastructure, good housing, education, health, low infant mortality); growth = change in real GDP per head; trade and technology create real wealth; more tax revenue for health, housing, education. AO3: growth is quantitative, living standards qualitative, so the link is unclear; more long-distance transport adds negative externalities; unclear how the benefits are used; cheap imports from low-income economies may raise unemployment; judgement on whether improvement is automatic (MS pp.16-17)
