parts.ask: Case 'Income inequality' (World Bank: the Gini coefficient fell by more than 5 points between 2008 and 2018 in Chile, Colombia and Mexico; stable in Ethiopia, India and Indonesia; rose in China and South Africa; unequal access to education for females is an obstacle to a more equal income distribution; Table 1.1 (CIA World Factbook), Gini / female-to-male literacy ratio / % below the poverty line: Brazil 0.53/1.01/4.2; Mauritius 0.36/0.95/10.3; India 0.35/0.90/21.9; Egypt 0.31/0.80/32.5; Pakistan 0.30/0.67/24.3; fiscal and supply-side policy as tools for changing the income distribution; limits of the Gini coefficient). Describe what is meant by the Gini coefficient and its possible range of values.
parts.final_form: three points: measure of income (or wealth) inequality; range 0-1 (0-100%); 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality
parts.ms: 1 measures income inequality (less commonly wealth distribution) in a population; 1 ranges from 0 (0%) to 1 (100%); 1 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality (MS p.7)
parts.er: Full marks needed all three aspects; a number confused which end of the range means perfect equality; some confused equality with equity (PER 2024-06 p.24).

parts.ask: Distinguish between absolute poverty and relative poverty.
parts.final_form: two definitions; absolute poverty tied to a poverty line or the World Bank definition
parts.ms: 1 absolute poverty = lacking the means to obtain the goods needed to sustain life; 1 below a 'poverty line' (income per day) / World Bank definition; 1 relative poverty = income compared with other groups in the same society (MS p.7)
parts.er: Generally well answered; many used the 'poverty line' or the World Bank definition of absolute poverty (PER 2024-06 p.24).

parts.ask: Consider whether Table 1.1 supports the conclusion that greater income inequality is linked to poor female-to-male literacy ratios and leads to greater poverty.
parts.final_form: data-based judgement that the table does not support the conclusion
parts.ms: 1 each: no apparent link to poor literacy ratios; better literacy ratios are in more unequal countries; cause and effect cannot be determined; higher Gini coefficients go with lower shares below the poverty line; no link to absolute poverty; no information on relative poverty; up to 2 for correct use of data (MS p.7)
parts.er: Not well answered: many wrongly said the table supports the conclusion. The table shows no link to absolute poverty, gives no relative-poverty data and no link to literacy ratios; up to 2 marks for using the data even with a wrong conclusion (PER 2024-06 p.24).

parts.ask: Use one example of a supply-side policy and one example of a fiscal policy to assess how a government might achieve greater equality in the distribution of income.
parts.final_form: for each policy: correct example, developed explanation, explicit link to equality of income distribution
parts.ms: Fiscal policy: correct example 1, development 2, link to equality 1; supply-side policy: correct example 1, development 2, link to equality 1 (MS p.7)
parts.er: Most chose progressive taxation and education/training; marks for correct identification and some development, but each policy needed a link to greater equality in income distribution (PER 2024-06 p.24).

parts.ask: Section B essay: the long-run equilibrium in perfect competition is often used to illustrate efficient resource allocation in a free market. Explain why this is so and consider what prevents efficiency from being achieved.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far efficiency is achievable in practice
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: allocative and productive efficiency; diagram and/or explanation of long-run equilibrium in perfect competition; efficiency prevented by market failure (excess profits, very large investment needs, externalities, merit goods, public goods); government intervention (regulation, taxation, subsidies, ownership) to restore efficiency. AO3: the concepts are mainly theoretical and rest on fine marginal calculations; intervention may not achieve efficiency (government failure) (MS p.8)
parts.er: Popular; good balanced answers used a diagram of the long-run equilibrium and discussed both productive and allocative efficiency, then market failure (externalities, merit goods, public goods) and intervention. Weakness: little evaluation, e.g. that perfect competition is a theoretical construct and intervention may itself fail; many did not develop the efficiency issue (PER 2024-06 pp.24-25).

parts.ask: Section B essay: using an indifference curve diagram, assess how far the effect of a price rise on demand differs between a normal good and a Giffen good.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the extent of the difference between the two goods
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: diagram with indifference curves and budget lines; budget line pivots for a price rise; consumption paths showing substitution and income effects for normal and Giffen goods; comment on the overall change in demand. Up to Level 2 only if no diagram. AO3: extent depends on price elasticity of demand and on the slope of the indifference curve / marginal rate of substitution (MS p.9)
parts.er: Those attempting it were well prepared with correctly labelled diagrams showing the direction of substitution and income effects for normal and Giffen goods; few addressed the extent of the change, so AO3 was missed (e.g. PED, slope of the IC, MRS). No diagram meant no marks above Level 2 (PER 2024-06 pp.24-25).

parts.ask: Section C essay: increased government spending is widely seen as a cause of economic growth, so it is sensible for a government to spend more because growth is good for its country. To what extent do you agree?
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on which side of the argument dominates
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: meaning and measurement of growth; extra government spending raises demand, allowing investment, research and output; actual vs potential growth; the multiplier; with little spare capacity, extra spending brings rising prices or more imports, harming the balance of payments and competitiveness; growth also depends on capital, skills, workforce, resources, finance, business structures, FDI, technology. AO3: both sides with a final conclusion on which dominates; issues: higher prices, income inequality, environmental degradation, over-use of scarce resources (MS p.10)
parts.er: Popular. Focused answers distinguished actual and potential growth and used the multiplier; balanced answers explaining why growth may not be good (demand-pull inflation with little spare capacity, more imports, factor quality, environmental damage) scored highly. Diagram opportunity: actual vs potential growth and macro trade-offs (PER 2024-06 pp.24-25).

parts.ask: Section C essay: national income statistics are often used to measure the standard of living. Consider to what extent they can be used to compare living standards between low-income and high-income countries.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far national income statistics allow valid comparisons
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define the standard of living; distinguish high- and low-income countries (per capita income); comparison problems: culture, climate, subsistence sector, informal economy, data collection, income distribution, exchange rates, purchasing power; which national income measure to use. AO3: assess the link between national income figures and living standards; alternative measures (MS p.11)
parts.er: Not popular. Expected definitions of national income, the standard of living and high vs low income; better answers explained comparison problems (culture, climate, subsistence, informal economy) and used GDP per head, inflation and employment trends; credit for evaluating the link to living standards; HDI and MEW were the usual alternatives (PER 2024-06 p.25).

parts.ask: Case 'Developments in the electric vehicle (EV) industry' (battery technology and economies of scale; Table 1.1 battery cost US$/kWh at annual output 0.5/2/4/10 million kWh: Technology A 115/105/98/97, Technology B 120/90/80/80; redundancies for ICE engineers in southern Germany; Saudi Arabia 45% of GNI from oil exports; Singapore fuel tax S$0.41 per litre, about 17% of price). Explain internal economies of scale, using an example from the information.
parts.final_form: definition (fall in long-run average cost as the firm's output rises) + one example from the text
parts.ms: 1 reduction in long-run average costs (LRAC); 1 as the firm increases its output; 1 technical or purchasing economies; 1 e.g. better electrode design from the information (max 3) (MS p.7)
parts.er: Many scored full marks; main errors were leaving 'long term' or 'average costs' out of the definition (PER 2024-06 p.26).

parts.ask: Consider what is meant by minimum efficient scale and to what extent the data in Table 1.1 suggest it has been achieved.
parts.final_form: definition + verdict per technology: A not reached, B may have been reached (cost flat at 80 from 4m to 10m kWh)
parts.ms: 1 MES = the first output on the LRAC curve at which further reductions in average cost stop; 1 Technology A suggests MES not reached; 1 Technology B suggests MES may have been reached (MS p.7)
parts.er: Very few had a clear idea of minimum efficient scale, but most applied it to the data and distinguished technologies A and B (PER 2024-06 p.26).

parts.ask: Analyse, with the aid of a diagram, the likely impact of the change to EVs on the labour market for workers producing ICE vehicles in southern Germany.
parts.final_form: labour-market diagram (demand D->D1, wage W->W1, employment L->L1) + structural/occupational unemployment + need for retraining
parts.ms: 1 unemployment is structural/occupational; 1 wages fall as demand falls; 1 need for retraining; diagram: 1 demand shifts D to D1; 1 wage falls W to W1 and employment L to L1 (or unemployment rises); 1 axes/labels (MS p.7)
parts.er: Diagram generally accurate (most scored 3 for it); comments on the diagram and text were weaker: some identified falling wages or structural unemployment, few saw the need for training; some wrongly labelled the labour-market diagram with AS and AD (PER 2024-06 p.26).

parts.ask: Evaluate the likely macroeconomic effects of the switch to EVs for both Saudi Arabia and Singapore.
parts.final_form: separate analysis for each country + a different evaluative comment for each
parts.ms: Saudi Arabia (max 3): exports fall; (X - M) and AD fall; output falls; government may raise G to offset; oil supply may be restricted to hold the price, so (X - M) indeterminate. Singapore (max 3): tax receipts fall; consumption pattern changes; government spending may fall; other taxes (goods or income) may rise; budget deficit. Evaluation 2: e.g. Singapore effect depends on whether electricity for EVs comes from non-oil sources; both depend on alternative tax revenue; needs a different evaluative comment for each country (MS p.8)
parts.er: Many good answers drew relevant points from the text, but few evaluated; a minority did not distinguish the two countries and treated them as affected in the same way (PER 2024-06 p.26).

parts.ask: Section B essay: market failure exists in all economies. Evaluate, with the aid of diagram(s), the meaning of market failure and two policies a government may use to correct market failure.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how effective the two chosen policies are
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: market failure as allocative or productive inefficiency or information failure; allocative efficiency (AR = MC or MSB = MSC) with diagram; productive inefficiency = not at minimum average cost; positive externalities -> under-consumption, negative -> over-production; policies: subsidies, indirect taxes, advertising, direct provision, price or quantity controls; labelled diagram of the externality and welfare change, redrawn for the chosen policy and referred to in the text. AO3: right subsidy/tax hard to measure; subsidies have an opportunity cost and need value judgements; time lags; advertising costly and uncertain; direct provision costly and possibly less efficient; net effect uncertain, depends on the good (MS pp.9-10)
parts.er: Very popular. Good answers defined allocative efficiency (diagram, or MC = MR or a variant) and explained its loss through externalities as the gap between private and social costs and benefits. Candidates who analysed exactly two policies answered in more depth than those who wrote all they knew about policies. Evaluation: stating that the effect depends on PED = E1; explaining how PED changes the outcome = E2 (PER 2024-06 p.27).

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate, with the aid of diagram(s), whether excess (supernormal) profit is always necessary for the continued existence of firms in perfect competition and monopoly.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether supernormal profit is 'always' necessary in each structure
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: definitions and assumptions of perfect competition and monopoly; short run vs long run; short-run equilibrium for both; supernormal profit possible in both in the short run; in the long run entry removes it for the competitive firm but not for the monopoly; SR and LR diagrams for both, referred to in the text. AO3: supernormal profit in perfect competition is transitory, a result of demand changes the firm reacts to at MR = MC; monopoly keeps long-run supernormal profit at MR = MC; can fund dynamic efficiency; monopolist may pursue sales revenue maximisation instead; natural monopoly may not earn supernormal profit; monopolies need not earn it (MS p.11)
parts.er: Diagrams of variable standard: MC must pass through minimum AC and profit maximisation must be at MR = MC, and many failed to show one or both. Better answers showed entry eroding excess profit in perfect competition and monopoly retaining it; evaluation was mostly limited to that contrast, and few asked whether a monopolist always earns excess profit (PER 2024-06 p.27).

parts.ask: Section C essay: in 2022 many countries had high inflation caused by supply disruptions (Covid-19, Russia-Ukraine conflict); in one country the government cut taxes and the central bank raised interest rates. Evaluate the likely impact of these policies on the government's ability to control inflation.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether these demand-side policies can control supply-caused inflation
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: the stated causes reduce supply, so cost-push/imported inflation; analysis through AS/AD or leakages and injections; a tax cut raises consumer demand or retained profits; higher interest rates reduce consumer demand or investment (transmission mechanism or AS/AD); effects on growth, unemployment and equality. AO3: accuracy of the size of the policy changes; time lags; expectations; the policies act on AD while the problem is supply shortages; short- and long-run effects on other aims; opportunity costs (MS pp.12-13)
parts.er: Reasonable analysis of basic fiscal and monetary effects; good answers applied it to the cost-push context and those who did not were limited; many used AD/AS diagrams; Phillips curve mentions were not applied. Good evaluation saw that the tax cut (and possibly the rate rise) suits demand-pull rather than cost-push inflation; analysis of supply-side policies or supply-side effects of the stated policies was appropriate (PER 2024-06 p.27).

parts.ask: Section C essay: evaluate the likely impact of globalisation on a low-income country's standard of living.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the balance of positive and negative effects on living standards
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: globalisation as world-wide flows of goods, services, capital and people and split manufacturing (phones, cars, football brands, law firms); low-income country defined; resource extraction vs manufacturing; standard of living material (real GNI per head) and non-material (social, health, education, working conditions); potential growth = PPF shift; funding through foreign aid, MNCs, commercial loans; investment raises national income (circular flow, multiplier, AD/AS) and affects employment, interest rates, balance of payments; AS/PPF effects. AO3: local industry destroyed, net job loss; local monopoly; MNC transfer pricing to tax havens cuts funds for education and health; low-skilled jobs, expatriates in skilled roles; resource exploitation disregarding local customs; private lenders reluctant to forgive debt; weigh positive and negative effects (MS pp.14-15)
parts.er: Many good answers: a clear statement of globalisation, then analysis of e.g. FDI on investment, employment, GDP, incomes and living standards; better answers used actual and potential growth; weaker answers never reached income or living standards. Good evaluation was rare; points such as resource exploitation were not developed through the negative externality (PER 2024-06 pp.27-28).

parts.ask: Case 'Income inequality' (World Bank: the Gini coefficient fell by more than 5 points between 2008 and 2018 in Chile, Colombia and Mexico; stable in Ethiopia, India and Indonesia; rose in China and South Africa; unequal access to education for females is an obstacle to a more equal income distribution; Table 1.1 (CIA World Factbook), Gini / female-to-male literacy ratio / % below the poverty line: Brazil 0.53/1.01/4.2; Mauritius 0.36/0.95/10.3; India 0.35/0.90/21.9; Egypt 0.31/0.80/32.5; Pakistan 0.30/0.67/24.3; fiscal and supply-side policy as tools for changing the income distribution; limits of the Gini coefficient). Describe what is meant by the Gini coefficient and its possible range of values.
parts.final_form: three points: measure of income (or wealth) inequality; range 0-1 (0-100%); 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality
parts.ms: 1 measures income inequality (less commonly wealth distribution) in a population; 1 ranges from 0 (0%) to 1 (100%); 1 0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality (MS p.7)
parts.er: Full marks needed all three aspects; a number confused which end of the range means perfect equality; some confused equality with equity (PER 2024-06 p.29). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Distinguish between absolute poverty and relative poverty.
parts.final_form: two definitions; absolute poverty tied to a poverty line or the World Bank definition
parts.ms: 1 absolute poverty = lacking the means to obtain the goods needed to sustain life; 1 below a 'poverty line' (income per day) / World Bank definition; 1 relative poverty = income compared with other groups in the same society (MS p.7)
parts.er: Generally well answered; many used the 'poverty line' or the World Bank definition of absolute poverty (PER 2024-06 p.29). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Consider whether Table 1.1 supports the conclusion that greater income inequality is linked to poor female-to-male literacy ratios and leads to greater poverty.
parts.final_form: data-based judgement that the table does not support the conclusion
parts.ms: 1 each: no apparent link to poor literacy ratios; better literacy ratios are in more unequal countries; cause and effect cannot be determined; higher Gini coefficients go with lower shares below the poverty line; no link to absolute poverty; no information on relative poverty; up to 2 for correct use of data (MS p.7)
parts.er: Not well answered: many wrongly said the table supports the conclusion. The table shows no link to absolute poverty, gives no relative-poverty data and no link to literacy ratios; up to 2 marks for using the data even with a wrong conclusion (PER 2024-06 p.29). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Use one example of a supply-side policy and one example of a fiscal policy to assess how a government might achieve greater equality in the distribution of income.
parts.final_form: for each policy: correct example, developed explanation, explicit link to equality of income distribution
parts.ms: Fiscal policy: correct example 1, development 2, link to equality 1; supply-side policy: correct example 1, development 2, link to equality 1 (MS p.7)
parts.er: Most chose progressive taxation and education/training; marks for correct identification and some development, but each policy needed a link to greater equality in income distribution (PER 2024-06 p.29). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section B essay: the long-run equilibrium in perfect competition is often used to illustrate efficient resource allocation in a free market. Explain why this is so and consider what prevents efficiency from being achieved.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far efficiency is achievable in practice
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: allocative and productive efficiency; diagram and/or explanation of long-run equilibrium in perfect competition; efficiency prevented by market failure (excess profits, very large investment needs, externalities, merit goods, public goods); government intervention (regulation, taxation, subsidies, ownership) to restore efficiency. AO3: the concepts are mainly theoretical and rest on fine marginal calculations; intervention may not achieve efficiency (government failure) (MS p.8)
parts.er: Popular; good balanced answers used a diagram of the long-run equilibrium and discussed both productive and allocative efficiency, then market failure (externalities, merit goods, public goods) and intervention. Weakness: little evaluation, e.g. that perfect competition is a theoretical construct and intervention may itself fail; many did not develop the efficiency issue (PER 2024-06 pp.29-30). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section B essay: using an indifference curve diagram, assess how far the effect of a price rise on demand differs between a normal good and a Giffen good.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the extent of the difference between the two goods
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: diagram with indifference curves and budget lines; budget line pivots for a price rise; consumption paths showing substitution and income effects for normal and Giffen goods; comment on the overall change in demand. Up to Level 2 only if no diagram. AO3: extent depends on price elasticity of demand and on the slope of the indifference curve / marginal rate of substitution (MS p.9)
parts.er: Those attempting it were well prepared with correctly labelled diagrams showing the direction of substitution and income effects for normal and Giffen goods; few addressed the extent of the change, so AO3 was missed (e.g. PED, slope of the IC, MRS). No diagram meant no marks above Level 2 (PER 2024-06 pp.29-30). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section C essay: increased government spending is widely seen as a cause of economic growth, so it is sensible for a government to spend more because growth is good for its country. To what extent do you agree?
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on which side of the argument dominates
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: meaning and measurement of growth; extra government spending raises demand, allowing investment, research and output; actual vs potential growth; the multiplier; with little spare capacity, extra spending brings rising prices or more imports, harming the balance of payments and competitiveness; growth also depends on capital, skills, workforce, resources, finance, business structures, FDI, technology. AO3: both sides with a final conclusion on which dominates; issues: higher prices, income inequality, environmental degradation, over-use of scarce resources (MS p.10)
parts.er: Popular. Focused answers distinguished actual and potential growth and used the multiplier; balanced answers explaining why growth may not be good (demand-pull inflation with little spare capacity, more imports, factor quality, environmental damage) scored highly. Diagram opportunity: actual vs potential growth and macro trade-offs (PER 2024-06 pp.29-30). [/43 PER section, identical to /41]

parts.ask: Section C essay: national income statistics are often used to measure the standard of living. Consider to what extent they can be used to compare living standards between low-income and high-income countries.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far national income statistics allow valid comparisons
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define the standard of living; distinguish high- and low-income countries (per capita income); comparison problems: culture, climate, subsistence sector, informal economy, data collection, income distribution, exchange rates, purchasing power; which national income measure to use. AO3: assess the link between national income figures and living standards; alternative measures (MS p.11)
parts.er: Not popular. Expected definitions of national income, the standard of living and high vs low income; better answers explained comparison problems (culture, climate, subsistence, informal economy) and used GDP per head, inflation and employment trends; credit for evaluating the link to living standards; HDI and MEW were the usual alternatives (PER 2024-06 p.30). parts.ask: Case 'The economic impact of extracting natural resources' (Ghana: offshore oil found 2007, extracted from 2010; multiplier; workers drawn from agriculture and manufacturing; 'Dutch disease'; oil tax revenue; Fig. 1.1 structure of goods exports 2007-2018; Table 1.1 2007 vs 2019: HDI 0.55->0.61, GNI per head PPP US$2,478->5,484, exchange rate printed as 'cedi per US$' 1.06->0.17). With the aid of a diagram, explain the effect of natural resource development on Ghana's potential growth.
parts.final_form: outward PPC or LRAS shift on a labelled diagram + statement that potential growth rises
parts.ms: 1 natural resource development increases potential growth; 1 PPC or LRAS moves outwards; 1 axes/labels; 1 shift in PPC or LRAS shown (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Explain how the extraction of natural resources in Ghana will 'create further employment in other sectors through the multiplier effect'.
parts.final_form: 2 marks multiplier theory + 2 marks application to the Ghana case
parts.ms: 1 multiplier = total increase in national income/output; 1 from an increase in injections into the circular flow; 1 the article identifies new jobs and their incomes; 1 these create further rounds of spending/jobs/income; 2 for understanding the multiplier + 2 for application (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Explain what the information means by the 'Dutch disease' and, using Fig. 1.1, consider to what extent Ghana suffered from it (Fig. 1.1, approximate reading of a 150 dpi page render: manufactures about 18-25% of goods exports in 2007-2010, about 10-17% in 2011-2017 and about 4% in 2018; fuel exports appear from 2011 at about 20-55%; agricultural raw materials and food fall from about 70% to 32-60%).
parts.final_form: mechanism (resource exports -> currency appreciation -> dearer manufactured exports -> lower manufacturing) + verdict using Fig. 1.1
parts.ms: 1 resource exports (Dutch natural gas) raised the exchange rate; 1 made manufactured exports dearer; 1 manufacturing output/exports fell; 1 manufactured exports fell from about 25% to less than 10%; 1 the chart supports the claim (max 4) (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Use the information to assess the impact of the extraction of oil on the standard of living in Ghana.
parts.final_form: define SoL (material and non-material), two-sided use of the data, conclusion that the data suggest improvement but are not definitive
parts.ms: 1 SoL = material and non-material well-being; for: jobs in oil and related industries 1, higher incomes 1, wider range of goods and services 1, GNI per head more than doubled 1, HDI improved (education, health) 1; against/limits: job losses elsewhere 1, no income-distribution data 1, working hours/leisure 1, oil pollution 1, Fig. 1.1 shows shares so employment changes by sector unknown 1; one-sided max 4; list max 4; conclusion 1: much suggests SoL improved but the data are not definitive (MS p.9)

parts.ask: Section B essay: governments promote policies to reduce the impact of negative externalities. Evaluate, using appropriate diagram(s), the extent to which two policies used to reduce negative externalities can also improve allocative efficiency.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far each of the two policies improves allocative efficiency
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define and explain negative externalities with examples; effects on output and price (over-production, under-pricing) and on allocative efficiency; identify, apply and analyse two policies (indirect taxation, subsidising alternatives, prohibition, better information, pollution permits). Maximum L2 if no diagram. AO3: direct cost of implementation; extent of the effect on allocative efficiency; effects on production costs and local employment; regressive or progressive income effects; information failure means the size of the externality is unknown (MS p.10)

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate the consequences for a firm's price and output if it changes its objective from profit maximisation to sales maximisation in response to the principal-agent problem.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on the price/output and welfare consequences of the switch
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define profit and sales maximisation; explain the principal-agent problem; profit maximisation at MR = MC with its equilibrium price and output; sales maximisation at AR = AC with its price and output; compare the two; relevant diagrams. AO3: profit maximisation gives a higher price and lower output than sales maximisation; consumers gain as producer surplus is transferred to them; greater equality; resources misdirected to sales-maximising firms, reducing allocative efficiency (MS p.11)

parts.ask: Section C essay: in periods of rising and persistent inflation, consumers and workers change their expectations of future inflation. Evaluate, with the help of diagram(s), the consequences of these changes in expectations for fiscal policy.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether fiscal policy can still reduce unemployment once expectations adjust
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define inflation and the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment; expectations based on past inflation; AD/AS analysis of cost-push and demand-pull inflation; Phillips curve trade-off becoming a wage-price spiral as workers seek compensation; fiscal policy's effect on unemployment and inflation; effect of changing expectations. Maximum L2 if no diagram. AO3: any fall in unemployment is temporary as workers bargain for higher wages; fiscal policy can no longer cut unemployment; shape of the short-run AS curve (Keynesians: more elastic); expansionary fiscal and monetary policy only raise inflation; Phillips curve may no longer hold (1970s high inflation and unemployment, 2000s low both); weaker unions now; global labour supply via trade and MNCs; growth and supply-side policies needed (MS pp.12-13)

parts.ask: Section C essay: many countries have joined or set up a free trade area (FTA). Evaluate, with the help of diagram(s), whether membership of an FTA is always beneficial to a country.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether FTA membership is 'always' beneficial
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define an FTA with examples; tariffs and non-tariff barriers and their effects; trade before and after; diagram of the effect on domestic output of removing the tariff and on consumer surplus; lower prices, more consumer surplus and allocative efficiency; economies of scale and productive efficiency. Maximum L2 if no diagram. AO3 micro: depends on PED/PES (inelastic -> small effects), strong preference for domestic goods; structural unemployment as demand switches to imports; polluting production may move to partners; cheaper inputs raise export competitiveness. AO3 macro: depends on marginal propensities to export and import, the net effect on (X - M) and AD, and multiplier effects of any net employment rise (MS p.14)

parts.ask: Case 'Reduced Migration to the United States (US)' (the migrant workforce grew by 0.6m a year until 2018; Covid-19 restrictions from 2019 stopped migration, so by 2022 nearly 2m fewer migrants were working than expected; half come as students, often in science, and stay to work in high-tech; well-educated immigrants are three times as likely to start businesses, so an estimated 200,000 fewer jobs; non-college migrants work in lower-paid retail, agriculture, hospitality and food services and send money home; more older US workers retiring at the same time; Mexicans and Central Americans over 35% of migrants, home incomes 10-20% of the US average; migrants earn 12% less than the average wage. Fig. 1.1 (2019) plots job vacancies by industry (%) against migrant share by industry (%) with a rising 'estimated relationship' line; approximate reading of a 110 dpi render: food about 26%/14.5%, hospitality about 23%/13%, high-tech about 15%/5.5%, education about 13%/1%, construction about 27.5%/3%, well below the line). Identify the relationship between the variables shown in Fig. 1.1 and suggest one possible reason for the relationship.
parts.final_form: positive (direct) relationship + one reason
parts.ms: 1 as the unfilled-job rate rises the foreign-born share of employment rises; 1 directly proportional; reasons 1 each: the US uses immigrants to fill labour shortages; immigrants are drawn to occupations with most vacancies; some such jobs are 'starter' jobs taken while looking for something better (max 2) (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Using a PPC diagram, explain the likely effect on US productive potential of stopping migration to the US from 2019 and of older US workers retiring.
parts.final_form: labelled PPC diagram + separate effect for each change (migration stop: PPC unchanged; retirement: PPC inwards)
parts.ms: 1 axes/labels; 1 shift from PPC to PPC1; 1 prevention of migration leaves the PPC unchanged; 1 retirement of older workers shifts the PPC left (inwards) (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Using the information and labour market theory, analyse why migrant workers in high-tech industries are likely to earn more than migrant workers in hospitality.
parts.final_form: demand-side (MPP/MRP) and supply-side (elasticity, numbers) reasoning; optional labelled demand-supply diagram
parts.ms: Demand: educated workers' MPP higher 1, value of their output higher 1, so higher demand and wages 1; some educated migrants become high-tech entrepreneurs earning profits 1; prejudice against less educated workers 1. Supply: slower immigration may narrow the low-paid gap 1 and widen the educated gap 1; unskilled labour supply wage-elastic 1, skilled inelastic 1; diagram: axes and labels 1, relevant S and D 1; migrants concentrated in areas -> over-supply cuts pay of the less educated 1 (max 6) (MS p.9)

parts.ask: Evaluate the likely impact of a return to pre-2019 migration levels on the macroeconomic performance of the US economy.
parts.final_form: AS and AD effects, BoP and employment, with a conclusion on the macro aims
parts.ms: 1+1 more labour -> AS rises, may stabilise prices; 1+1 AD rises as migrants spend (high MPC, strong multiplier); 1+1 remittances reduce (X - M), worsening the BoP; 1+1 domestic employment rises as immigrants set up businesses; 2 crowding-out argument (immigrants take domestic jobs) needs reasoned support; 1+1 both AD and AS rise, raising GDP, which refutes crowding out; diagram 1+1; max 7 for content; 1 conclusion: growth aim met, BoP probably worse, employment up (MS p.10)

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate whether marginal utility theory can fully explain the link between a change in a good's price and the quantity demanded of that good.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether MU theory 'fully' explains the price-quantity link
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define marginal and total utility; diminishing marginal utility; effect of a price change through the equi-marginal principle, with a diagram; downward-sloping demand curve, valid for normal and inferior (non-Giffen) goods but not distinguishing them. AO3: is the consumer rational (imperfect information, bounded rationality, advertising); cannot separate income and substitution effects, so cannot explain Giffen goods; ceteris paribus unrealistic, each change needs a new demand schedule; assumes constant marginal utility of money; struggles with one-off purchases such as a house (MS p.11)

parts.ask: Section B essay: the IMF and World Bank often require privatisation before offering loans, grants or debt relief. Evaluate the view that privatisation will always improve the allocation of resources in a country.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether privatisation 'always' improves resource allocation
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define privatisation (sale of state-owned firms; may include private provision of services); productive and allocative efficiency, X-inefficiency; market-structure models to analyse efficiency after privatisation; market economy; benefits: more competition, shareholder scrutiny, wider access to funds; compare monopoly with more competitive models; correct diagrams referred to in the text; less government financing; sale proceeds to repay debt or fund education and health; loss-making industries no longer funded by taxpayers. AO3: judge against productive, allocative and dynamic efficiency; break-up of natural monopolies ('final mile' problem); state monopoly replaced by private monopoly behind high barriers; need for regulators; equity: profits lost to the state; job losses raise the fiscal burden; private firms ignore externalities (MS pp.12-13)

parts.ask: Section C essay: Mexico 2020 data: GNI 18.5 billion pesos; nominal wages +2.8%; disposable income +1.2%; unemployment 4.2%; population growth 1.1%; inflation 3.4%. Evaluate the use of these statistics in assessing the standard of living in Mexico in 2020.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on how far these statistics can show Mexico's standard of living
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: material and non-material standard of living and GNI; define each statistic; what each value implies; developed links between each statistic and living standards. AO3: no time comparison, so improvement cannot be judged; population size and a price index are needed to get real GNI per head; wages, disposable income and unemployment indicate material change; nominal wage growth (2.8%) below inflation (3.4%) means real incomes fell; other measures needed for non-material aspects (education, health, life expectancy, hours worked: HDI, MEW, MPI) (MS p.14)

parts.ask: Section C essay: between 2010 and 2020 very low interest rates encouraged low-income countries to borrow from foreign investors and governments to finance long-term growth. Evaluate this approach to promoting long-term economic growth.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a justified judgement on whether foreign borrowing is a sound route to long-term growth
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: long-term growth as more inputs and an outward PPC shift, measured by real GDP; low incomes mean low savings, so foreign finance is needed; lenders: governments (e.g. China's Belt and Road), agencies (IBRD), sovereign wealth funds; MNC investment in plant and machinery; AS/AD analysis; projects must earn a return (marginal efficiency of capital) above the interest rate; rising (US$) interest rates bring falling exchange rates, dearer debt service, worse (X - M); IMF/World Bank lending accepted. AO3: share of foreign vs local funding; quality of projects ('roads to nowhere' vanity projects); lender-sourced construction and materials weaken the current account; higher rates in high-income countries raise the cost and opportunity cost of borrowing; commodity price slumps depreciate the currency and raise repayments (MS pp.15-16)

parts.ask: Case 'The threat from large firms' (The Guardian 2021: one US technology company averaged sales of US$1.2bn a day, earning the average US salary of US$52,000 in under four seconds; five of the largest firms made combined profits of over US$68bn, helped by pandemic online working and shopping, welcomed by many at home; critics: a handful of super-powerful firms will dominate, bad for consumers and competition, causing unacceptable inequality; one firm tried to stop workers joining a union; huge cash reserves let them undercut possible entrants; investors wary of backing competitors and new owners sell out to dominant firms; political power, tax avoidance, expansion into similar markets; Schumpeter's 'creative destruction'; from 'pirates' to a 'navy'). Distinguish between limit pricing and predatory pricing.
parts.final_form: two definitions, each explained and developed (2 + 2)
parts.ms: limit pricing: an incumbent sets a price low enough (close to average cost, normal profit) to deter new entrants (1 + 1 development); predatory pricing: a price below unit cost in the short run to force an existing rival out, then raised to recover the losses; anti-competitive and illegal under anti-trust law (1 + 1) (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Explain whether there is any evidence in the article of these two types of pricing policy.
parts.final_form: evidence for each type taken from the article
parts.ms: limit pricing: yes, investors will not back new companies and potential owners sell to the large firms (1); new owners leaving the industry might be described as predatory pricing (1); 'Must explain both types from the article to gain 2 marks' (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Assess three possible positive effects on the macroeconomy of the huge increase in the size of the five largest technology companies.
parts.final_form: three macroeconomic effects, each identified and developed (2 each); micro effects not credited
parts.ms: any three, 2 each (effect + development): more employment; higher aggregate demand; economic growth; possible economic development; multiplier effects; relevant comments on inflation and the balance of payments also credited; 'Must assess effects on macro economy not micro economy' (MS p.8)

parts.ask: The article claims that the growth of large firms harms consumers and competition and causes inequality. Consider whether the article and economic theory support this claim.
parts.final_form: support from the article and theory (max 4), counter-evidence from the article and theory (max 4), conclusion that the statement is not always true (1); max 8
parts.ms: for (max 4): article - profits compared with salaries, restriction on union membership, tax avoidance, expansion into adjacent markets; theory - less choice, higher prices, restricted output, higher profits, monopoly, small firms forced out; against (max 4): article - consumers at home welcomed the services; theory - economies of scale, lower prices, innovation and research; conclusion: the statement is not always true (1); max 8. The MS stem reads 'article or by economic theory' (MS p.9)

parts.ask: Section B essay: market failure arises from negative production externalities. With the help of a diagram, assess how far introducing an indirect tax is likely to correct this cause of market failure.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); tax-on-externality diagram required; ends with a judgement on indirect taxation compared with alternatives
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: market failure as allocative inefficiency, efficient output where AR = MC; negative externality as social cost above private cost ('spill-over'); labelled diagram of an indirect tax shifting the private cost curve and its effect on output and efficiency; links from the tax to firms' behaviour and removal of the externality. Cap: 'L2 max if no or incorrect diagram provided'. AO3: the right tax is hard to set without side effects such as unemployment; effects take time; inelastic demand limits the output effect; costly, bureaucratic, hard to monitor and enforce; pollution permits may work better; indirect taxes are regressive; conclusion comparing alternatives (MS pp.10-11)

parts.ask: Section B essay: evaluate, with the help of a diagram, the claim that a perfectly competitive labour market always pays higher wages than a monopsony labour market.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); monopsony (and competitive) labour-market diagrams required; ends with a conclusion testing 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: features of a perfectly competitive labour market, with diagram; how a monopsony sets wages; monopsony diagram showing wage and employment; factors affecting labour demand and supply in both markets. Cap: 'L2 max if no or incorrect diagram provided'. AO3: trade unions and government intervention change outcomes; union-backed training may raise productivity and wages; capital-labour substitutability and capital intensity; a minimum wage in monopsony may be set above the competitive wage; unions can raise monopsony wages through collective bargaining; high competitive wages attract more labour supply in the long run; conclusion testing 'always' (MS pp.12-13)

parts.ask: Section C essay: central banks can control the money supply; an increase in the money supply will cause inflation; therefore central banks can control inflation. Evaluate this statement.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); ends with a judgement on how far monetary policy can control inflation
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: define inflation; components of the money supply (commercial bank balances at the central bank plus bank deposits); central bank instruments: open market operations/quantitative easing and interest rates; links from money supply or interest rates to inflation; how specific instruments cut the money supply (e.g. selling long-term government securities reduces bank deposits); effects on AD and inflation. AO3: the money supply is hard to define and measure; the money-price link is unclear; the interest rate-money supply link is unclear (higher rates may raise saving and so deposits); effectiveness depends on the cause of inflation, and demand-pull may be better tackled by contractionary fiscal policy; conclusion on how far monetary policy controls inflation (MS pp.14-15)

parts.ask: Section C essay: some high-income countries have introduced high tariffs on some imports to reduce the negative effects of globalisation on their economies. With the help of a diagram, evaluate this policy.
parts.final_form: 20-mark essay, no parts: AO1+AO2 /14 (MS Table A: L1 1-5, L2 6-10, L3 11-14) + AO3 /6 (Table B: L1 1-3, L2 4-6); tariff diagram required; ends with a cost-benefit judgement on the net effect for the high-income economy
parts.ms: AO1/AO2: globalisation (free trade, capital and labour mobility, technology transfer); characteristics of high-income countries; a main negative effect is low-cost imports raising unemployment; labelled tariff diagram and analysis of selective tariffs; effects on stakeholders, e.g. tariff revenue reinvested for long-term growth. Cap: 'L2 max if no or incorrect diagram provided'. AO3: retaliation and trade war; trade diversion, lower allocative and productive efficiency, net welfare loss; higher prices for consumers and producers; higher costs may cut demand and raise unemployment; loss of globalisation's benefits such as choice; protecting inefficient firms harms the long run; conclusion using cost-benefit analysis (MS pp.16-17)

parts.ask: Explain what is meant by an optimum population.
parts.final_form: definition with both elements: maximum income per head AND given resources/technology
parts.ms: population that, with existing resources/factors/state of technology (1), gives the highest income per head / maximum standard of living (1)
parts.er: both marks needed income per head at its highest AND the given resources/technology assumption; omitting the assumption gave 1; rewording 'optimum' as 'best' or 'ideal' level of population scored 0 (PER p.8)

parts.ask: Explain how China's population structure changed between 1970 and 2020 and consider whether Fig. 1.1 supports the statement 'its population is decreasing'.
parts.final_form: structure changes (not size) plus a reading of the graph: growth rate falling but level still rising
parts.ms: structure: declining birth rate (1), ageing population (1), rising dependency ratio (1); Fig. 1.1 shows population still growing, at a slower rate, up to 2020 (1), so it does not support 'its population is decreasing' (1)
parts.er: poorly answered: most described changes in the size of the population instead of its 'structure' (birth rate, ageing, dependency ratio); most wrongly said the graph showed decline - better answers saw the growth rate falling while the level still rose (PER p.8)

parts.ask: Identify two economists' observations about changes in China's population and analyse how each would affect GDP.
parts.final_form: two observations, each developed to a final effect on GDP
parts.ms: fewer young people (1) -> smaller pool of innovators/entrepreneurs (1) -> lower output and productivity, GDP falls (1); relatively more older people (1) -> more spending on social services (1) -> more transfer payments, larger budget deficit, negative effect on GDP (1)
parts.er: many scored full marks; 1 for each identification and 2 for development - full marks required stating the final impact on GDP (PER pp.8-9)

parts.ask: Consider the effects on the economy of the population policies suggested by China's government (as opposed to economists' 'alarming statements').
parts.final_form: effects of the one-child and two-child policies (3 each) plus a conclusion (1)
parts.ms: one-child policy: based on population above the optimum and a shift to a skills-based economy (1); slowed population growth but raised dependency (1), may cut saving and investment (1), lowering long-run AS and AD (1); two-child policy (2016): to restore growth and move towards the optimum (1), needs a young skilled workforce with technology (1), more competitive (1), raising AD and AS long run (1); max 3 per policy; conclusion (1), e.g. Fig. 1.1 suggests the two-child aims are unlikely to be met. MS also lists raising fertility, raising the retirement age, skills/technology, and boosting domestic consumption
parts.er: over 90% discussed raising the retirement age, which the PER says was not China's government policy and earned no marks (note: the MS bullet list does include it); expected: one-child and two-child policies, 3 marks each; very few wrote a conclusion (PER p.9)

parts.ask: Evaluate the claim that oligopolies can avoid price competition while keeping supernormal profits in the long run.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: oligopoly characteristics; kinked demand curve and price rigidity; game theory - stable prices via Nash equilibrium; entry barriers, collusion and limit pricing sustain long-run abnormal profit; non-price competition as an alternative. AO3: collusion often illegal and hard to sustain; contestability legislation erodes barriers; prolonged limit pricing cuts short-run profit, investment and dynamic efficiency; non-price competition (advertising, differentiation) is costly; some firms prefer break-even pricing to gain market share; conclusion.
parts.er: many detailed answers; best drew an accurate labelled kinked demand curve, linked it to price rigidity and price leadership, and added non-price competition and limit pricing; game theory often not linked to collusion and long-run supernormal profit; few gained high AO3 - mostly cursory comments on collusion breaking down, rarely break-even pricing or the cost of non-price competition (PER p.9)

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate the consequences of an effective minimum wage for employment and the wage level in a monopsony labour market.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; monopsony diagram (MCL above ACL=S, MRP) required; microeconomic answer only
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: features of monopsony; meaning of minimum wage; accurate labelled monopsony diagram with the minimum wage; effect on labour supply and demand; new employment level and wage. Cap: 'L2 Max if no relevant diagram provided.' AO3: outcome depends on relative elasticities of labour demand and supply; size of the rise; higher wage may raise productivity and MRP; small firms may close; costs reduce global competitiveness; capital-labour substitutability; judgement on the net effect on wages and employment.
parts.er: many ignored the key words: macro discussion (e.g. inflation) gained nothing; the overwhelming majority drew a perfectly competitive labour-market diagram instead of a monopsony one, giving wrong predictions about employment; better answers drew an accurate monopsony diagram and reasoned from it, with evaluation on elasticities and capital substitution; far too many stayed in Level 1 (PER p.9)

parts.ask: With a diagram, assess the effectiveness of government policies that might be used to reduce demand-pull inflation.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; AD/AS diagram required
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: causes of demand-pull inflation and why inflation is a problem; Keynesian or monetarist analysis with labelled diagram; fiscal policy to cut AD (e.g. higher direct tax); monetary policy - higher interest rates, revaluation, open market operations; supply-side policies accepted. Cap: 'L2 Max if no relevant diagram provided'. AO3: higher direct tax may hurt growth/employment; cuts to education and health harm long-run welfare; effect depends on the state of the economy; revaluation may worsen the BoP (Marshall-Lerner) and cost export jobs; high interest rates cut investment and long-run growth; house-price falls; conclusion comparing short and long run.
parts.er: about 90% chose it and most scored highly on AO1/AO2 with Keynesian and monetarist policies and accurate diagrams; micro diagrams instead of AD/AS held marks down - a correct diagram is essential for Level 3 when one is asked for; evaluation of revaluation using Marshall-Lerner and the reverse J-curve scored well, evaluation of Keynesian policies was often one-sentence (Level 1); conclusions generally good (PER p.10)

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate the effectiveness of expenditure-switching policies in reducing a current account deficit.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; at least two expenditure-switching policies and a labelled diagram (e.g. tariff) for L3
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: meaning of a current account deficit; expenditure switching via relative prices of imports and exports; examples - tariffs, devaluation in a fixed system (export subsidies/supply side accepted); labelled tariff diagram and its effect on the current account and on domestic suppliers, consumers and firms; analysis of a second policy. Cap: 'L2 max if no relevant diagram provided.' AO3: size and persistence of the deficit; retaliation; cost-push inflation; net welfare loss of a tariff (shown on a diagram); devaluation depends on elasticities - Marshall-Lerner; devaluation may cause demand-pull or cost-push inflation; conclusion on the statement.
parts.er: few answered; Level 3 needed at least two expenditure-switching policies plus a relevant labelled diagram - many discussed tariffs without the standard tariff diagram; good answers used devaluation with J-curve evaluation; retaliation rarely developed; welfare loss of tariffs almost always missed; supply-side points should separate short-run from long-run effects; conclusions often just summaries (PER p.10)

parts.ms: 2015 Paris Agreement: willing to raise green energy output or cut fossil-fuel use (1); by 2022 more emphasis on economic growth / continued fossil-fuel energy (1); promised funds from rich to poor countries did not materialise, or poor countries less effective at cutting CO2 (1)

parts.ask: Evaluate the claim that growth of a firm by takeover is desirable because consumers get lower prices and the firm gains extra profits.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must weigh both 'lower prices' and 'additional profits'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: takeover as external growth; takeover (one firm buys another) vs merger (two firms form one new company); horizontal and vertical integration; economies of scale from horizontal integration lower costs and prices; backward/forward vertical integration gives further cost savings; higher market share and total revenue raise profits. AO3: cost savings may not be passed on; more monopoly power lets the firm restrict output and raise prices; takeovers can be costly and cut long-run profits; communication problems and culture clashes (diseconomies of scale); competition authorities may intervene with price regulation; conclusion addressing 'low consumer prices' and 'increased profits'.

parts.ask: A country has stagflation (high inflation with a negative output gap): with a diagram, evaluate the effectiveness of fiscal policy in solving this problem.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; AD/AS (or Keynesian cross) diagram showing the gap and the policy
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define inflation and its problems; negative output gap explained and identified on a labelled AD/AS diagram; meaning of fiscal policy and how it can close the gap or reduce inflation (diagrams); AD/AS analysis of why high inflation and a negative gap coexist (e.g. AS shift); 'Accept Keynesian Cross diagram'; 'Maximum 8 marks if no relevant diagram'. AO3: contractionary fiscal policy cuts inflation but widens the gap, and vice versa; supply-side measures raise AS, lower inflation and close the gap in the long run but productivity investment may cost jobs in the short run; fiscal policy may need pairing with supply-side reforms; crowding out; conclusion comparing short-run and long-run effectiveness.

parts.ask: Evaluate the claim that a free trade area gets all the benefits of a customs union while avoiding all its costs.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address the 'all benefits / all costs' claim
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: free trade area = removal of tariffs/quotas between members; customs union = internal free trade plus a common external tariff; FTA gains: specialisation, faster growth, lower costs to firms, higher incomes, competition, productivity; customs union: shared protection from outsiders plus a large single market; trade creation when internal tariffs go. AO3: customs-union costs - loss of economic and political sovereignty, trade diversion under a common external tariff (misallocation of world resources); but integration can bring growth from comparative advantage, political stability and inward FDI; non-tariff barriers; judgement on how far an FTA really avoids the costs while getting the same benefits.

parts.final_form: one-sentence definition plus one example from the data
parts.ms: definition (1): current economic activity that does not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their needs; illustration (1): switching from coal to alternative fuel sources to avoid environmental damage

parts.ask: Use the information to comment on the possible effects on the economies of the countries that refused to sign the carbon (coal) agreement.
parts.final_form: advantages and disadvantages, each point with its consequence
parts.ms: they are top coal producers (1); advantages: cheap power (1) sustains GDP/growth (1); reliable power (1) keeps production going (1); coal can be stored (1) to meet electricity demand (1); disadvantages: finite resource (1) so future switching costs (1); continued negative externalities (1), e.g. CO2/greenhouse/toxic gases, poorer air (1); max 4

parts.ask: Discuss why the article calls China 'a country of contradictions'.
parts.final_form: contrast of coal dependence with green investment
parts.ms: undermines the summit aim by using mainly coal (70%) for electricity (1), large share of world emissions (31%) (1), coal use set to hit a record in 2022 (1), will not sacrifice growth (8.3%) (1) - max 2; but invests in solar, wind, hydro (1), leading user of electric cars and maker/exporter of wind turbines (1) - max 2; refuses to sign the agreement (1)

parts.ask: With a marginal social cost and benefit diagram, discuss whether continued use of coal to generate electricity makes allocative efficiency less likely.
parts.final_form: labelled MSC/MPC/MPB=MSB diagram with Q* and Q, explanation and conclusion
parts.ms: definitions: private cost (1), external/social cost (1), allocative efficiency (1); external costs of coal - greenhouse gases, pollution (1); data: 3 countries produce 52% of coal CO2 (1); diagram: correct axes and labels of MPB/MSB, MSC, MPC (1), externality/welfare loss shown (1), Q* and Q identified (1); MSC > MPC because of negative externalities (1); conclusion: efficient output is Q* not Q, so allocative efficiency is not achieved (1)

parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: features of a perfectly competitive labour market; meaning of an increase in labour productivity; diagram of wage determination in the market and the firm, effect of productivity on wage and employment; comparison with an imperfect (monopsony) market and its equilibrium. parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; labelled IC/budget-line diagram with substitution and income effects
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: indifference curve and map; budget line and how price or real-income changes move it; consumer equilibrium (tangency) shown on a diagram; effect of a price change on equilibrium; both substitution and real-income effects needed for Level 3. Cap: 'No diagram-highest mark is L2 – 8'. AO3: shape depends on assumptions about behaviour (satisfaction-maximising); assumes consumers can rank bundles; only two goods while real consumers compare many prices; advertising can change tastes and the curves; conclusion on how well the analysis predicts the effect of a price change.

parts.ask: Evaluate the claim that growth of a firm by takeover is desirable because consumers get lower prices and the firm gains extra profits.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must weigh both 'lower prices' and 'additional profits'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: takeover as external growth; takeover (one firm buys another) vs merger (two firms form one new company); horizontal and vertical integration; economies of scale from horizontal integration lower costs and prices; backward/forward vertical integration gives further cost savings; higher market share and total revenue raise profits. AO3: cost savings may not be passed on; more monopoly power lets the firm restrict output and raise prices; takeovers can be costly and cut long-run profits; communication problems and culture clashes (diseconomies of scale); competition authorities may intervene with price regulation; conclusion addressing 'low consumer prices' and 'increased profits'.

parts.ask: A country has stagflation (high inflation with a negative output gap): with a diagram, evaluate the effectiveness of fiscal policy in solving this problem.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; AD/AS (or Keynesian cross) diagram showing the gap and the policy
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define inflation and its problems; negative output gap explained and identified on a labelled AD/AS diagram; meaning of fiscal policy and how it can close the gap or reduce inflation (diagrams); AD/AS analysis of why high inflation and a negative gap coexist (e.g. AS shift); 'Accept Keynesian Cross diagram'; 'Maximum 8 marks if no relevant diagram'. AO3: contractionary fiscal policy cuts inflation but widens the gap, and vice versa; supply-side measures raise AS, lower inflation and close the gap in the long run but productivity investment may cost jobs in the short run; fiscal policy may need pairing with supply-side reforms; crowding out; conclusion comparing short-run and long-run effectiveness.

parts.ask: Evaluate the claim that a free trade area gets all the benefits of a customs union while avoiding all its costs.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address the 'all benefits / all costs' claim
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: free trade area = removal of tariffs/quotas between members; customs union = internal free trade plus a common external tariff; FTA gains: specialisation, faster growth, lower costs to firms, higher incomes, competition, productivity; customs union: shared protection from outsiders plus a large single market; trade creation when internal tariffs go. AO3: customs-union costs - loss of economic and political sovereignty, trade diversion under a common external tariff (misallocation of world resources); but integration can bring growth from comparative advantage, political stability and inward FDI; non-tariff barriers; judgement on how far an FTA really avoids the costs while getting the same benefits.

parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; diagram required
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: productive efficiency (minimum AC) and allocative efficiency shown; perfect-competition equilibrium as the efficient benchmark; sources of market failure: negative/positive externalities, information failure (merit/demerit goods), missing public and quasi-public goods, monopoly power (higher price, lower output), factor immobility, equity concerns; a chosen policy from the 8.1.1 list (taxes, subsidies, price controls, quotas, regulation, direct provision, permits, property rights, nationalisation/privatisation, information, nudges). AO3: opportunity cost of the policy; can the government measure the failure; unintended consequences, regulatory capture, bureaucracy, political interference; budget implications; evaluation through an example.

parts.ask: Evaluate whether marginal revenue product (MRP) theory always explains differences in wages.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: MRP = MPP x price as the demand side of the labour market; what affects MPP; effect of product-market structure on MRP; labour supply factors (population, age structure, working conditions, education/experience, migration); demand and supply together set the wage. AO3: theory assumes perfect competition; employers cannot easily know individual MRP when work is collaborative; productivity hard to measure (health, education) and some output has no market price; trade unions; government intervention (minimum wage, staffing ratios); other causes of differentials - discrimination, segmented markets, capital equipment, monopsony.

parts.ask: Market failure causes climate change and inefficient allocation, and government intervention is the only solution: assess how far you agree.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; the conclusion must weigh the word 'only'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: climate change as market failure (allocative efficiency where MSB = MSC); negative externality MSC > MPC so greenhouse-gas output is too high; forms of intervention: subsidies for cleaner consumption/production, advertising, direct provision (e.g. alternative transport), indirect tax on the CO2 source, nudges; labelled externality diagram showing market vs optimum output, welfare loss and the policy's effect, referred to in the text. parts.ask: With diagram(s), evaluate the claim that the degree of competition a firm faces is determined only by the barriers to entry into its market.

parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: types of entry barriers and their effect on market structure; detailed analysis of at least two structures, one without barriers (perfect or monopolistic competition) and one with (oligopoly or monopoly), covering product, knowledge and profit levels; correctly labelled diagrams referred to in the answer. Caps: 'Max L2 if no diagram'; 'Max L2 if only one type of structure'. AO3: barriers limit the number of firms so the claim is partly right; low-barrier structures are highly competitive; oligopolists still compete through product differentiation and marketing; monopolies are limited by contestability and by regulation.

parts.ask: Evaluate the effect of a rise in the exchange rate on the achievement of a country's macroeconomic aims.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; at least two macro aims developed
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: appreciation raises export prices and lowers import prices, so X falls, M rises, (X-M) and AD fall, trade balance may worsen; injections/leakages; AD/AS diagram or multiplier/45-degree analysis of national income and growth (actual vs potential); 'Minimum of 2 aims developed for L3'. MS examples use the US dollar but say 'OR any other currency'. AO3: why the currency rose; price elasticity of demand for exports; extent of the effect on employment and inflation; reserve-currency status; size of the mpm and multiplier; capital inflows/MNCs; share of (X-M) in GDP.

parts.ask: Evaluate the statement that economic growth can only occur when an economy is below full employment.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define economic growth (rise in real GDP over time) and full employment (resources fully used; natural rate of unemployment remains); below full employment growth comes from higher AD using spare capacity (movement towards the PPF, little inflation); at full employment growth only through potential growth: LRAS/PPF shift from productivity, technology, education, capital; AD-AS diagram for movement along AS and an LRAS-shift diagram. AO3: statement too narrow - growth possible below (actual) and at full employment (potential); recession vs long run; AD-led growth near full employment brings inflation not real growth; multiplier size; whether C, I or (X-M) can rise without unemployment; MS judgement: statement 'partially correct'.

parts.final_form: short explanation
parts.ms: GDP = total output within a country (1); constant prices remove the effect of price changes (1) so the real change in output is measured (1); easier comparison of GDP (over time) (1)

parts.ask: Explain one possible benefit of horizontal integration and one possible benefit of vertical integration (large commodity traders).
parts.final_form: two definitions, each with one benefit
parts.ms: horizontal integration defined (1) + a benefit (1); vertical integration defined (1) + a benefit (1)

parts.ask: Describe how the market structure of individual farmers is likely to differ from that of the commodity traders.
parts.final_form: name each structure and give its features
parts.ms: farmers: monopolistic competition (1), many sellers, similar product, no entry barriers (MS also lists 'price maker') - max 3; traders: oligopoly (1), few (four) sellers, barriers to entry, price maker, product differentiation - max 3; 'Market structure must be correct to gain explanation marks.'

parts.ask: Use the article to evaluate the impact of developing agriculture and mining on the standard of living in Brazil.
parts.final_form: data-based evaluation ending in a judgement that the evidence is mixed/incomplete
parts.ms: define standard of living: monetary (1) and non-monetary (1) (max 2); data interpretation max 4: improvement - GDP up $0.7tn (1), GDP per head up $1459 (1), large exporter (max 2); reduction - rainforest degradation from agriculture/mining/oil (1), pollution and flooding from burst dams (1) (max 2); no data on non-financial aspects such as education, health, housing (max 2); conclusion: data mixed, wider data needed for a full judgement (1)

parts.ask: Traffic congestion causes allocative inefficiency: with diagram(s), evaluate two policies a government may use to reduce it.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; exactly two policies analysed and evaluated, with diagram(s)
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define allocative efficiency (MSB = MSC, consumer satisfaction maximised); congestion as a negative consumption externality (MPB > MSB) causing over-consumption; intervention options: subsidies to alternative transport, advertising alternatives, direct provision of alternatives, indirect taxation, nudges; labelled diagram of market vs optimum output and welfare loss, redrawn to show the policy, referred to in the text. AO3: subsidy size hard to measure, opportunity cost and value judgement; demand for public transport/alternatives may be price-inelastic; time lags; advertising costly and uncertain; public provision costly and may be less efficient.

parts.ask: Chief executives earn over 100 times the average wage of their employees: assess how economic theory can account for this difference.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: wages set by demand and supply of labour; demand from MRP = MPP x P; supply depends on skills, education, training, ability and elasticity of supply; why wages differ with MRP and supply; economic rent; apply to the CEO vs worker labour markets and compare them. AO3: MPP is hard to measure; CEO pay is often set by people in similar positions and may be inflated; monopsony employers may underpay workers; prejudice and discrimination lower some wages.

parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; at least two macro aims analysed
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: depreciation/devaluation lowers export prices and raises import prices; effect on (X-M) and AD, injections/leakages; AD/AS diagram or multiplier/45-degree diagram for national income and growth; identify at least two aims (BoP, growth, inflation, employment) and analyse the effect on at least two. AO3: whether domestic supply capacity can respond; exports of agricultural commodities price-inelastic in supply; short-run gain in employment vs higher inflation (Phillips curve); debt servicing easier if debt is in domestic currency, harder if in foreign currency; FDI/MNC inflows; trade's share of GDP.

parts.ask: Evaluate whether the presence of multinational companies (MNCs) in low-income countries is always beneficial.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define MNC and low-income country; benefits: infrastructure, jobs, training, higher GDP/GNI, wider range of products, better living standards; actual growth via AD/AS; current and capital account flows and the exchange rate; employment gains and losses, structural unemployment; potential growth via resource development, education, infrastructure (PPC shifts out). AO3: MNC output may displace local producers; changes to work and cultural practices and non-material living standards; corruption of officials; capital-intensive methods may raise unemployment; production/consumption externalities; raw-material exports and 'Dutch' disease (high exchange rate hurting other exports, structural unemployment).
