parts.ask: With a diagram, explain the link between a Gini coefficient and a Lorenz curve (article quotes global Gini 0.75 in 1975, 0.67 in 2022).
parts.final_form: labelled Lorenz curve diagram plus the Gini formula and its 0-1 interpretation
parts.ms: accurately labelled Lorenz curve (2); formula showing how the Gini coefficient is calculated (1) (MS does not print the formula; the usual one is area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the whole area under the line of equality); Gini measures how unequal the distribution of income/wealth is (1); 0 = perfect equality (1); 1 = perfect inequality (1); max 5

parts.ask: Distinguish between equity and equality.
parts.final_form: two contrasted one-line definitions
parts.ms: equality generally refers to equal opportunity (1); equity refers to achieving fairer outcomes (1) (MS wording)

parts.ask: Analyse whether the newspaper's claim that global inequality fell conflicts with Table 1.1 (China and India Gini rose 1990-2016).
parts.final_form: balanced analysis of conflict / no conflict using the figures
parts.ms: some limited supporting evidence (1); text is a global average while the table is for particular countries (1); text shows inequality falling, Gini down (1) but the table shows Gini rising in China and India (1); no conflict on national income: both show incomes rising (1)

parts.ask: Explain globalisation and, using the article, assess whether there is enough evidence that globalisation brings a net benefit for everyone.
parts.final_form: definition, evidence for and against, and a judgement on the sufficiency of the evidence
parts.ms: definition: growing interdependence of economies, cultures and populations through cross-border trade, technology and flows of investment, people and information (2); benefits in the article: higher incomes, life expectancy (+10 years in sub-Saharan Africa), literacy, less absolute poverty, lower inequality (2); drawbacks: environment, exploitation of workers, domestic unemployment, dependence on other countries (2); evaluation: gains came while population grew, but no statistics to weigh benefits against costs and 'net benefit' is ambiguous, so an overall assessment is hard (2)

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate the impact on consumers and producers of an increase in market contestability.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; must cover both consumers and producers
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: contestability = how open a market is to new entry; factors limiting it, e.g. barriers, especially high sunk costs; non-contestable market shown by a labelled profit-maximising oligopoly or monopoly diagram; removing barriers gives consumers lower prices and more choice; firms' supernormal profits fall; incentive to cut unit costs and avoid X-inefficiency. Cap: 'No diagram L2 Max'. AO3: lost market share may cut economies of scale so lower prices not passed on; depends on the degree of contestability and whether it lasts; natural monopolies unlikely to gain; lower profits may reduce dynamic efficiency; conclusion on net benefit to consumers and/or producers.

parts.ask: With a diagram, assess the importance of labour supply for wage and employment levels of firms in perfectly competitive and in monopsony labour markets.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; both market types must be analysed for L3
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: features of a perfectly competitive labour market; why the firm faces a perfectly elastic labour supply and how it meets MRP to set employment; diagram of wage and employment for such a firm; monopsony: upward-sloping supply (AC of labour) with MC of labour above it, employment where MC of labour = MRP, so wage and employment are lower than the competitive outcome. Caps: 'No diagram L2 Max'; 'Must refer to both markets for L3'. AO3: market-wide productivity rise or labour shortage still raises the competitive wage; within-firm productivity rise raises employment not the wage; minimum wage or trade union can make monopsony supply perfectly elastic at a higher wage and raise employment; conclusion.

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate the effectiveness of using monetary policy to increase the rate of economic growth in a country.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: types of monetary policy (money supply, interest rates, exchange rate policy); meaning and importance of economic growth; labelled AD/AS diagram linking higher AD to higher real GDP; money supply up -> interest rates down -> investment and consumption up -> AD and GDP up; devaluation for export-led growth. MS note: 'No diagram Max L3'. AO3: impact depends on spare capacity; liquidity trap or interest-inelastic MEC; negative expectations; devaluation works only if net trade rises (Marshall-Lerner); inflation risk; stagflation trade-off, supply-side policy better long term; conclusion comparing short-run and long-run effectiveness.

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate the statement that tariffs are the most effective way to correct a balance of payments deficit.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; macro diagram required
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: tariff = tax on selected imports, a barrier to free trade; outline of BoP accounts; deficit and its link to the exchange rate; labelled diagram as the basis for analysing the tariff's BoP effect; tariff as expenditure-switching, depending on the price elasticity of demand for imports; effect mainly on the goods and services part of the current account. Cap: 'No diagram Max L3' with 'Micro diagram not acceptable'. AO3: retaliation; depends on whether the deficit is persistent or temporary; expenditure-reducing policy may be better (e.g. with high inflation); inelastic imports raise import spending; loss of consumer and producer surplus; judgement on short-run vs long-run impact.

parts.ask: Explain the meaning of 'allocative efficiency and productive efficiency'.
parts.final_form: two definitions, each with its condition
parts.ms: allocative: producing what consumers want (1), where P = MC / AR = MC (1); productive: producing with the least use of resources (1), at minimum average cost (1); producing on the PPC (1)

parts.ask: Explain what is meant by a negative production externality.
parts.final_form: definition naming a cost and the third party
parts.ms: a cost (1) borne by someone other than the producer/a third party (1)

parts.ask: Identify from the extract one negative production externality of steel production.
parts.final_form: one item from the extract
parts.ms: noise, dirt or polluted air (1); max 1

parts.ask: With a diagram, explain the consequences for output and price if the steel market has to take its negative production externalities into account.
parts.final_form: MPC/MSC/MPB diagram with the change in P and Q stated
parts.ms: labels (1), axes (1) and explicit indication of the negative externality (MSC above MPC) (1); output falls from Q to Q1 and price rises from P to P1 (1)(1); welfare loss explained (1)

parts.ask: Consider whether 'a monopoly always operates against the interests of the consumer'.
parts.final_form: two-sided argument ending in a conclusion that addresses always
parts.ms: for monopoly: economies of scale, R&D investment, natural monopoly (e.g. railways) - point + explanation each (max 4); against: loss of productive, allocative and dynamic efficiency - point + explanation each, or a diagram showing loss of AE and PE: axes/labels (1), correct cost and revenue curves (1), loss of AE (1), loss of PE (1) (max 4); max 7 for argument; conclusion (1)

parts.ask: With a diagram, evaluate whether diminishing marginal utility theory adequately explains the market demand curve for all goods and services.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address 'all goods and services'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: assumptions (rational consumers who prefer more to less, two-good world, substitutable goods, perfect knowledge); define marginal and total utility; diminishing marginal utility; how quantity bought changes with price; equi-marginal principle (MU/P equalised) as one price changes; horizontal summation of individual demand curves gives market demand. AO3: rationality assumption unrealistic; no income and substitution effects, so cannot explain inferior (or Giffen) goods; indivisible, infrequent purchases (a fridge vs weeks of food) do not fit; real consumers buy many goods, not two.

parts.ask: With diagrams, evaluate the claim that subnormal and supernormal profits occur only in the short run and only for firms in perfect competition.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; diagrams of perfect competition and at least one other structure expected
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define short run, subnormal and supernormal profit; conditions of perfect competition; how both profits arise in perfect competition in the short run and are removed by entry/exit to normal profit in the long run; relevant diagram. AO3: monopolistic competition also shows short-run sub/supernormal profit resolved to normal profit; monopoly can keep supernormal profit in the long run; oligopoly may or may not earn sub/supernormal profit in both short and long run.

parts.ask: A country imposes a 20% tariff on imports and restricts immigration: with diagram(s), evaluate the impact of these two policies on its inflation rate.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; both policies analysed
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define a tariff; it raises the price of imported consumer goods directly and the cost of imported raw materials (cost-push inflation); AS shifts left; restricting immigration reduces labour supply and prevents wages falling (or raises them), also cost-push; diagram of the tariff on prices, of labour supply and wages, or of AS shifting. AO3: elasticity of supply of domestic substitutes; whether domestic workers will do the jobs; inflation also depends on AD - fewer immigrants means less demand and less demand-pull inflation; limited migration lets domestic workers win higher wages (cost-push).

parts.ask: Evaluate whether an increase in a government's budget deficit will always lead to economic growth.
parts.final_form: continuous essay (no parts); AO1+AO2 /14 by Table A levels, AO3 /6 by Table B; needs a justified conclusion that answers the specific question; conclusion must address 'always'
parts.ms: AO1/AO2 indicative: define budget deficit and economic growth; AD/AS or 45-degree analysis; circular flow: higher G raises AD; short-run vs long-run growth; effects on employment, inflation and the BoP; supply-side spending (education, investment) from the deficit. AO3: closeness to full employment; Phillips curve and inflation; size of mpc and the multiplier; expectations; the multiplier is a short-run (trade-cycle) effect, the accelerator and an outward PPC shift are needed for long-run growth.
